catalogTitle: כשלומד תורה משיג אלקות' ויש יחוד בינו ובין ה' יותר מבעוה"ב .

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains how a Jew who learns Torah and does mitzvos truly grasps and unites with Hashem Himself, because Hashem contracted His will and wisdom into the halachos, a union greater than anything in Olam Haba.

abstract.en: The Rav returns to the Tanya's claim that through Torah and mitzvos all ten faculties of the soul unite with Hashem, and asks how this is possible when Hashem is the Ein Sof whom no thought can grasp. Intellect, he explains, is simply not the sense that perceives Hashem. The answer is tzimtzum: Hashem contracted His will and wisdom into the mitzvos and their halachos, as a scientist carries radioactive material in a lead container. How much light a person receives depends on how he learns. The Torah descended like water, level by level, until it was clothed in thought, speech and physical action. After a long digression on the body as the seat of the ten faculties and on refining the middos during Sefirah, he explains why one hour of Torah and mitzvos in this world exceeds all of Olam Haba, and closes with the parable of embracing the king.

en: Hashem is beyond all grasp of thought, not because human intellect is too weak but because intellect is not the sense that perceives Him.
Hashem contracted His will and wisdom into the 613 mitzvos and their halachos, so that one who understands a halachah grasps Hashem Himself, clothed in a garment.
How much divine light fills the vessel of Torah depends on how the person learns: with fear of Heaven and honor for the Torah, or lightheadedly.
The Torah descended like water from its high place, level by level through the worlds, until it was clothed in physical things, so that every thought, word and action can take hold of it.
One hour of Torah and mitzvos in this world exceeds all of Olam Haba, because there one enjoys only the radiance of the Shechinah, while here one is united with Hashem Himself.

title.en: How can one unite with the Ein Sof?

summary.en: The Rav recalls that through Torah and mitzvos all faculties of the soul unite with Hashem, and asks how this can be when Hashem is the Ein Sof whom no thought grasps. He explains that intellect is not the sense for perceiving Hashem, as a watch cannot understand its maker, and that even His will and wisdom are beyond understanding.

title.en: Hashem's wisdom contracted into the halachos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Tanya that where one finds Hashem's greatness one finds His humility: He contracted His will and wisdom into the mitzvos and halachos. With the parable of radioactive material carried in a lead container, he explains that one who understands a halachah holds Hashem Himself in his mind, clothed in garments, and that the lowest halachos hold the greatest holiness.

title.en: Each word of Torah is a vessel for light

summary.en: The Rav explains that every word of Torah is a vessel that holds divine light, and how much light enters depends on the learner. One who learns with fear of Heaven and honor receives the light; one who learns lightheadedly has an empty vessel; even learning not for its own sake, aiming to reach lishmah, has its place, and great tzaddikim drew great powers from their Torah.

title.en: The Torah descends like water

summary.en: The Rav reads on in the Tanya: Hashem contracted Himself into the mitzvos so that every mind can grasp them, and the ten faculties of the soul are clothed in the three garments of thought, speech and action. He explains the Midrash comparing Torah to water that flows to the lowest place, the chain of worlds down to parchment and ink, and how the ten faculties correspond to the parts of the body, as in Pesach Eliyahu.

title.en: Refining the middos in the days of Sefirah

summary.en: In a digression, the Rav explains that during the weeks of Sefirah one refines the middos, which are rooted in the limbs of the body, so as to receive the Torah on Shavuos. He shows that the laws of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah fall in the sedras read in these weeks, and brings Rabbi Chaim Vital that without good middos one cannot receive the Torah, along with Pirkei Avos and the Bnei Yissaschar.

title.en: Greater than all of Olam Haba

summary.en: The Rav explains that through Torah and mitzvos the whole body is wrapped in the 'bundle of life' with Hashem, and therefore Chazal say one hour in this world is better than all of Olam Haba. In Olam Haba one enjoys only the radiance of the Shechinah, like the sun's rays, while here Hashem gives Himself in tangible form through physical mitzvos.

title.en: Embracing the King through His garments

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's parable of one who embraces the king: though the king is clothed in garments, it is truly the king he embraces. He brings 'His right hand embraces me' and 'Let Him kiss me with the kisses of His mouth', asks why the passuk says the right hand, and answers that Torah comes from chesed and water, which is the right side. He concludes that the union of this world exceeds that of Olam Haba.

catalogTitle: פרקי אבות: The Greatness of the חכמי התורה and the קדושה that Exists in their names

oneLiner.en: Learning the opening of the sixth perek of Pirkei Avos, the Rav explains that the very names of the Chachamim are Torah, because a Jewish name is the substance of the neshamah, and mentioning it connects the learner to the Tanna himself.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by comparing the exile of Klal Yisrael to Adam HaRishon's exile from Gan Eden, and says that young people, who are still in their own Gan Eden, have the opportunity to learn. He introduces the sixth perek of Avos, braisos about Torah written in the language of the Mishnah. Words of Torah said with ruach hakodesh contain far more than their plain meaning, so several explanations of one phrase are all true. He asks why the Gemara spends so much time repeating the names of the Chachamim, and answers that the name itself is Torah. Speech is powerful, as shown by the fruit of Eretz Yisrael in the days of the Midbar. He tells how Rav Shimon Sofer silenced scoffers in Krakow with a story about a holy name, brings the Mishnah's mention of Chevron on Yom Kippur, and explains with Adam's naming of the animals that a name holds a being's essence. Finally he explains why the Tanna does not spell out the reward of Torah lishmah: Olam Haba is too holy even for the Nevi'im to see.

en: Words of Torah said with ruach hakodesh contain much in few words, so several explanations of the same Chazal can all be true.
Mentioning the name of a Chacham is not an interruption in learning, because the name itself has become Torah.
Every word a Jew speaks has an effect in the world and above it: a good word builds and brings blessing, a bad word destroys.
A Jewish name is made of holy letters that are the substance of the neshamah, so mentioning a Tanna's name activates his neshamah and connects the learner to him.
The Tanna does not spell out the 'many things' that one who learns Torah lishmah merits, because his Olam Haba is too holy for even the Nevi'im to see.

title.en: Galus, youth, and the sixth perek

summary.en: The Rav compares Klal Yisrael's exile from Eretz Yisrael to Adam HaRishon's exile from Gan Eden, and says young people are still in their Gan Eden and can learn. He introduces the sixth perek of Avos, added before Shavuos, made of braisos about Torah written in the language of the Mishnah.

title.en: Why mention the names of the Chachamim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Torah said with ruach hakodesh contains much in few words, so several explanations are all true. He asks why so much time is spent repeating the names of the Chachamim, and answers that the name itself is Torah, reading 'baruch shebachar bahem' as praise of the one who devotes himself to them.

title.en: The power of speech

summary.en: The Rav explains that every word a Jew says reaches the heavens: a good word brings light and bounty, a bad word destroys. He points to the huge fruit the meraglim brought back while Klal Yisrael learned Torah in the Midbar, and to Rashi's reading of 'yadber' as leading.

title.en: Rav Shimon Sofer and the holy name

summary.en: The Rav says mentioning a tzaddik's name gives a hold on him, and that tzaddikim accomplished things through holy names. He tells how Rav Shimon Sofer, facing scoffers at his first drasha in Krakow, told of the Shabbos-desecrating factory owner in his father the Chasam Sofer's city whose factory burned when he pronounced a name his father taught him.

title.en: Chevron on Yom Kippur; a name is the neshamah

summary.en: The Rav brings that Moshe Rabbeinu killed the Mitzri with a holy name and that a tzaddik's name brings down chesed. He cites the Gemara asking why the announcement on Yom Kippur morning mentioned Chevron, and answers that naming the city of the Avos draws down rachamim; all the more the name of a Chacham, which is his very neshamah.

title.en: Adam's names and Rabbi Meir's neshamah

summary.en: The Rav tells that the Chiddushei HaRim told a father to name his child himself so he would merit ruach hakodesh. He explains that Adam HaRishon named each creature by the letters it is made of, as with the aryeh, and that Rabbi Meir judged people by their names; so saying 'Rabbi Meir' before his halacha draws his neshamah into the learner and makes the halacha easier to understand.

title.en: Torah lishmah merits many things

summary.en: The Rav goes through the braisa that one who learns Torah lishmah merits many things and is lifted above all creation. He asks why the Tanna does not say what the many things are, and answers that the Nevi'im described only the reward of those who help the talmid chacham; his own Olam Haba is too great for a living person to behold.

title.en: The holier, the easier to spoil

summary.en: The Rav explains with the yayin hameshumar that the holier something is, the more easily it is spoiled: levels of tumah, meat versus vegetables, and wine that a goy touches. Olam Haba is so holy and so opposed to this world that no eye may see it, which is why the Tanna cannot describe it.

catalogTitle: כל אחד זוכה להאור שבתורה לפי קדושתו ומדרגתו.

oneLiner.en: Building on the Derech Hashem and Tanya chapter 5, the Rav explains that Torah draws down G-dliness only when learned with awe and by an upright Jew, each according to his level, and that understanding a halacha unites a person with Hashem's wisdom more deeply than any other mitzvah.

abstract.en: The Rav recalls from chapter 4 that Torah and mitzvos are vessels for Hashem's light, and brings the Derech Hashem: every person, through Torah and mitzvos, draws holy influence into himself and into all creation, but on two conditions. The first is learning with seriousness and derech eretz, not lightheadedly; here he discusses dress while learning, tells of the Arugas Habosem, and warns against copying a rebbe's faults, citing the four kinds of students in Avos. The second is being an upright Jew, though even a rasha's Torah keeps a trace of holiness. After the parable of the esrog, he learns Tanya chapter 5: the intellect grasps what it understands and is enclothed in it, so understanding a halacha grasps Hashem's will, a unity greater than any mitzvah. He compares sod and pshat, explains Torah as the soul's bread, and closes with a story from R' Yitzchak Chayes.

en: Through Torah and mitzvos every Jew draws holy influence into himself and into all of creation, each according to the reach of his soul.
According to the Derech Hashem, Torah draws down holiness only when learned with awe, seriousness and derech eretz, and by a person who is not a rasha.
Words of Torah are vessels for G-dliness, like a lamp that gives light only when connected to the current.
Even Torah learned without the proper way keeps some holiness of its own, like a body that keeps a trace of the soul.
Tanya chapter 5 teaches that when one understands a halacha, his intellect grasps Hashem's will and is enclothed in it, a two-way unity found in no physical thing.
The unity of Torah study surpasses that of mitzvos: a mitzvah enclothes a person from outside, while Torah is taken inside, like bread that becomes part of the body.

title.en: Torah and mitzvos draw light into all creation

summary.en: The Rav recalls chapter 4, that Torah and mitzvos are vessels for Hashem's holiness, and brings the Derech Hashem: through them each person draws holy influence into himself and into all creation, some tzaddikim to the point of bringing a city, a country or the world to teshuvah.

title.en: First condition: learning with awe; the Arugas Habosem

summary.en: The Rav brings the Derech Hashem's first condition, that Torah be learned with seriousness and awe, not sprawled out lightheadedly, and discusses how people dress while learning. He tells how a fellow student found the Arugas Habosem learning on a hot day fully dressed, and the Arugas Habosem answered that he had learned other things from their Rebbe.

title.en: Learning the good from a rebbe, not the faults

summary.en: Using the four kinds of students in Avos, the Rav warns against picking out a rebbe's apparent faults, such as the Ohev Yisroel's eating or R' Baruch's anger, which had hidden reasons. He explains that chassidim in Eretz Yisroel learn in shirtsleeves because of the hot climate of their origins, while the common rule is derech eretz for Torah.

title.en: Respect for seforim; the lamp and the current

summary.en: The Rav brings the Derech Hashem that one must honor the seforim and speak respectfully of the Rishonim; learning without derech eretz draws nothing. Torah words are vessels in which Hashem contracts Himself, and like a lamp not plugged in, they give no light when learned without awe.

title.en: Second condition; each according to his level; the esrog

summary.en: The second condition is that the learner not be a rasha, yet even a rasha's Torah has a trace of holiness that brings him back, like a body that keeps a trace of its soul; each person draws according to his level. The Rav then explains why an esrog worth twenty cents costs a hundred and fifty dollars: G-dliness is enclothed in it, so holding it one holds G-dliness.

title.en: Tanya ch. 5: intellect, knower and known

summary.en: The Rav begins Tanya chapter 5 on the term 'grasping', and explains the three terms sechel, maskil and muskal. The intellect grasps and surrounds what it understands, and at the same time is enclothed in it, as one absorbed in a Tosfos does not hear when called: a two-way unity.

title.en: Halacha as Hashem's will; a wondrous unity

summary.en: The Rav explains that every halacha, even about cases that may never occur, is Hashem's wisdom and will; when one understands it clearly, he grasps what no thought can grasp, like embracing the king through his garments. This is a unity with nothing like it in the physical world, greater than that of mitzvos, which enclothe a person only from outside.

title.en: Mitzvos with kavanah; sod versus pshat

summary.en: The Rav notes that a mitzvah done with kavanah also includes Torah, but the Tanya speaks of the bare act. He then explains that each grasps Torah according to his intellect in pshat, remez, drash and sod: sod is higher because it has fewer garments, yet a clearly understood Gemara gives a stronger unity, since no one fully grasps the secrets of the Torah.

title.en: Torah as bread; mitzvos as garments

summary.en: The Rav explains why Torah is called bread that nourishes the soul when learned in depth, and brings the Zohar that in the world of souls Torah is food and mitzvos are garments. He brings R' Pinchas of Koretz on why mitzvos cost money and Torah is free, tells of R' Yitzchak Chayes who appeared to his son in fine garments but without shoes, and closes urging both collecting for Jews and learning Torah lishmah.

catalogTitle: עשר כתרין דמסאבותא כנגד עשר ספירות דקדושה. ביאור טעם שהטומאה נקראת כתרין.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter six, the Rav explains that the ten powers of kedushah have a counterpart of ten 'crowns' of impurity, why impurity is called crowns and sitra achra, and how a Jew elevates kelipas noga by doing even permitted things for the sake of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the principle 'zeh l'umas zeh asah ha'Elokim': Hashem keeps kedushah and impurity in balance, and only one who takes Hashem with him tips the scale. He illustrates this with the Gemara about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya, a Midrash about the Satan at the births of the Avos, and the great sorcerers of earlier times. He then reads Tanya chapter six: just as the G-dly soul has ten holy sefiros, the Jew's animal soul from kelipas noga has ten powers of impurity. Using a walnut's four shells, the laws of orlah, milah and periah, and the Masorah's siman for Parshas Kedoshim, he shows that only a Jew can elevate noga. He explains why impurity is called 'crowns' rather than sefiros, how intellect shapes the middos, why there is no neutral reshus, and, with a vort of the Kotzker Rebbe, why impurity is called the 'other side'.

en: Hashem made kedushah and impurity in balance, 'zeh l'umas zeh'; only by taking Hashem along does a person tip the balance toward kedushah.
Just as the G-dly soul has ten holy sefiros clothed in thought, speech and action, the animal soul from kelipas noga has ten powers of impurity: seven bad middos and an intellect divided into three.

A Jew's animal soul is from kelipas noga, which can be turned to kedushah when he eats and does physical things for the sake of Heaven; a gentile's comes from the three wholly impure kelipos, which cannot.
Impurity is called 'crowns' and not sefiros because a sefirah is transparent and nullified to Hashem, while each power of impurity declares 'I will reign'.
There is no neutral middle: a permitted act not done for Heaven's sake joins the side of impurity, which is why it is called sitra achra, the 'other side'.

title.en: Zeh l'umas zeh: kedushah and impurity in balance

summary.en: The Rav recalls the previous perek on the union with Hashem through Torah and mitzvos, then opens chapter six with 'zeh l'umas zeh asah ha'Elokim'. He brings the Gemara about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the minim, and concludes that kedushah and impurity are balanced, and Hashem tips the scale for one who takes Him along.

title.en: The Satan's share, Esav and the great sorcerers

summary.en: The Rav brings a Midrash that the Satan demanded a share at the births of the Avos, and that Esav, the admoni, was born with Yaakov; David too was admoni, but with fine eyes. He then explains that when there were great tzaddikim there were also great sorcerers like Bilaam and Amalek, while today both sides are small, and that a union exists in impurity as in kedushah.

title.en: Ten sefiros of the soul and ten of impurity

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of Tanya chapter six: as the G-dly soul consists of ten sefiros clothed in three garments, the soul of the sitra achra from kelipas noga has ten powers of impurity, seven bad middos with a mind that gives birth to them. He mentions that in the days of sefirah one asks to refine each middah through the mitzvah of counting.

title.en: Kelipas noga: the walnut, orlah and periah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jew's animal soul is from kelipas noga, which can be elevated, and illustrates the four kelipos with the four shells of a walnut. He shows the same pattern in 'kedoshim tihyu' as the Ramban explains it, in orlah and its fourth year, and in milah and periah, and notes that the Masorah's siman for the 64 pesukim of Parshas Kedoshim is 'noga'.

title.en: Bnei Keturah: milah without periah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that the Bnei Keturah are obligated in milah, and the Acharonim who say only milah and not periah, since periah was given only in the days of Yehoshua. The inner reason is that a gentile's soul comes from the three impure kelipos and cannot elevate noga, which is also why only a Jew brings shelamim, as the Midrash on 'uri tzafon' shows.

title.en: Why impurity is called 'crowns'

summary.en: The Rav rereads the Tanya and asks why the ten powers of impurity are called crowns and not sefiros. A sefirah, like 'livnas hasapir', is transparent and lets the light of kedushah through, which is bittul; impurity says 'I am something' and 'I will reign'. He links the ten powers of impurity to the ten sons of Haman.

title.en: The mind behind the middos; garments of impurity

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's point that the middos follow the intellect: a child and an adult have the same middah of love, but a small mind directs it to toys and a large one to property. He then explains the three garments of impurity, thought, speech and action not for Hashem, and 'all that is done under the sun', which is futility and a broken spirit.

title.en: No neutral reshus: the 'other side'

summary.en: The Rav explains that there is no middle between mitzvah and aveirah: eating or business done for Heaven's sake raises noga to kedushah, and otherwise it joins impurity. He brings the Kotzker Rebbe on the Targum's 'l'tzad' in 'al tigshu el ishah', that there are two sides of a fence, and concludes with the Tanya that kedushah rests only on what is nullified to Hashem.

catalogTitle: ישראל בטל לה' בעצם' ומקבל מצד הקדושה' הסיטרא אחרא ישות ואינו בטל לה'' ומקבל בבחינת אחוריים.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, on Tanya chapter 6, that holiness is whatever is nullified to Hashem and receives from Him face to face, while the sitra achra is self-standing 'something' that receives its life only from behind and in hiding.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Tanya's teaching that the Shechinah rests on ten Jews, because ten is the number of bitul: in a minyan each Jew loses his separate identity and becomes part of one unit. He supports this from the numbers of the tribes, which always ended in tens and hundreds, and from the minyan being learned from the meraglim, explaining that only the good part of Jews joins together, while evil, like the goyim, cannot unite, since holiness is unity and klipah is separation. He then explains that whatever says 'I am something' occupies space and pushes Hashem away, as with the ba'al ga'avah, unlike the Aron that took up no space. Hashem gives life to everything at every moment, but to the sitra achra only from behind, through man, who is a small world. He ends with the two levels of klipos, the three impure ones and klipas nogah, shown in the walnut, milah, orlah, the siddur and Yechezkel's vision.

en: The Shechinah rests on ten Jews because in a minyan each one is nullified and they become one unit of holiness.
Holiness is unity and klipah is separation, so only the good part of Jews can join together, and evil, even ten wrongdoers together, never forms a minyan.
Whoever considers himself 'something' occupies space and pushes Hashem away, so the revelation of Hashem is absent from him, measure for measure.
Hashem creates the world anew at every moment, and even the klipos and the wicked receive their life from Him, only in hiding.
Holiness receives face to face, while the sitra achra receives from 'behind', through a long descent of contractions.
Man, made in the image of G-d, is a small world, and through him the shefa reaches all of creation, including the sitra achra.
The klipos have two levels: three wholly impure ones that must be cut off, and klipas nogah, which can be subdued and turned to holiness.

title.en: Ten as the number of bitul

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya that the Shechinah rests on ten, because there the Jews are nullified into one. He explains why the four compartments of tefillin are learned from foreign languages, and that ten is written as one with a zero, the many nullified to the one.

title.en: Ten Jews, the tribes and the meraglim

summary.en: The Rav brings the saying that where ten Jews are, even without learning Torah, angels cannot enter, and ties ten to the ten utterances of creation. He shows that the census of the tribes always ended in tens, and asks why the minyan is learned from the wicked meraglim.

title.en: Holiness unites, klipah separates

summary.en: The Rav answers that in ten Jews each loses his identity and they form one unit, which goyim cannot do, since klipah is a world of separation. Only the good part of each Jew joins, as the chelbonah in the ketores shows, and so even the meraglim formed a minyan through their inner good.

title.en: The proud man occupies space

summary.en: The Rav reads that whatever is not nullified does not receive from the inner holiness. Hashem fills every place, but He is revealed only where there is bitul; the ba'al ga'avah who says 'I am something' occupies space, unlike the Aron, which miraculously took up no space, and so Hashem leaves him, measure for measure.

title.en: Constant creation, like electricity

summary.en: The Rav explains that even where the sitra achra is, Hashem's kingship is there in hiding, since He creates the world anew at every moment, as electricity must be generated constantly for a lamp to burn. Even klipos, wild animals and the wicked receive shefa at every moment, but with hester panim.

title.en: Face to face and from behind

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the face-to-face bond of holiness with giving over the shoulder to someone one does not like. He reads the Tanya that what is not nullified receives only from 'behind', through descent upon descent and contraction upon contraction, until it can exist as a separate thing.

title.en: Man as a small world

summary.en: The Rav explains that man holds the key to creation and channels shefa to it through his mitzvos, his 248 limbs and 365 sinews matching the mitzvos. Man is a microcosm: his face forms Hashem's name, his mouth is a patach, the vowel of chochmah, and the world in turn has eyes, a mouth and a heart, Yerushalayim.

title.en: How the sitra achra is fed

summary.en: The Rav explains that the sitra achra also needs sustenance, and it receives from 'behind', from the waste left when the good of food is separated, in the place where holiness cannot be. Deep within are sparks of holiness in exile, like the Jews in galus, and therefore this world is called the world of klipos, with only islands of holiness.

title.en: The two levels of klipos

summary.en: The Rav shows that in this world evil is the majority and holiness the minority. He explains the three impure klipos and klipas nogah through the four layers of a walnut, milah, orlah, the nusach of Velamalshinim and Yechezkel's vision, and closes with wishes for receiving the Torah with joy.

catalogTitle: נביא: A Deeper Explanation of the Story of נבות היזרעאלי & his כרם

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that everything a person receives, from food to talents to a vineyard, carries sparks of his own soul and comes to him for his mission, and from this he explains why Navos lost his life and his vineyard and why Achav and Izevel wanted it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Chasam Sofer on the weeping 'for their families' in Beha'aloscha: the people wanted meat to elevate relatives reincarnated in animals. From the Borei Nefashos blessing and the Ba'al Shem Tov he develops that every food and possession holds sparks of a person's own soul, which only he can elevate. He then tells the story of Navos and brings the Midrash that Navos, a gifted singer, stopped going up to Yerushalayim to sing, and so lost his life. The Rav explains: singing was Navos's mission, and the vineyard, source of wine and song, was his tool; a worker who does not work is dismissed, and the idle vineyard itself accused him. He ties song to Shabbos, David HaMelech and the matching of a chasunah, explains why Achav and Izevel were drawn to the vineyard and how it brought Achav to teshuvah, and closes with Yehoyachin's food and the call to eat and use everything for Hashem.

en: Every food and object a person uses holds sparks of holiness that belong to his own soul, and by eating with a brachah and using the strength for Torah and mitzvos he elevates them.
Hashem sends each person down on a specific mission and supplies him with the tools for it: money, objects, talents and food.
Navos was given a voice and a vineyard for his mission of singing; when he stopped singing he lost both, not as a punishment but because he was no longer fulfilling his purpose.
Achav could only obtain the vineyard because it also held a part of his soul; one who takes what is his dishonestly would have received it honestly had he waited.
The vineyard of song brought Achav to teshuvah, since the gate of song is next to the gate of teshuvah.
Yehoyachin knew that his food came from Hashem, the true King, and not from the king of Bavel; the whole redemption depends on bringing every spark to its tikkun.

title.en: Weeping for their families; sparks in food

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that the people who wept 'for their families' wanted meat to elevate relatives who died in Mitzrayim and were reincarnated in animals. He explains the Borei Nefashos blessing: Hashem creates people with needs and fills them with what is exclusively theirs, because fragments of holiness that fell through the sin of Adam are held in the food.

title.en: Everything a person uses is his own

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's answer to why Hashem made people hungry: the food holds sparks of the eater's soul that must return to him and are elevated when he eats properly and serves Hashem with the strength. He adds the Arizal on 'not by bread alone', and explains with an apple cut in half that each person's food, possessions and even his wife are part of his soul, given to him as a shaliach.

title.en: The story of Navos and the Midrash

summary.en: The Rav tells how Achav coveted Navos's vineyard, Navos refused, and Izevel had false witnesses testify so that Navos was killed, after which Eliyahu confronted Achav. He then brings the Midrash on 'honor Hashem from your wealth', read as 'from your throat': Navos had a wonderful voice, stopped going up to Yerushalayim to sing, and for this he was killed.

title.en: The vineyard as the tool of song

summary.en: The Rav asks why the attribute of judgment was so demanding, and answers that each person is sent on a mission and given the tools for it. A vineyard produces wine and wine produces song, and the word kerem itself alludes to this; so Navos, whose mission was to sing and gladden Jews, was given a vineyard as part of his soul, and when he did not sing he had no reason to live.

title.en: The idle worker and the accusing vineyard

summary.en: With a parable of a factory owner who dismisses not only a thief but also a worker who sits idle, the Rav explains that Navos's soul came down from the Kisei HaKavod to sing, and his death was not a punishment but the end of a life that served no purpose. The vineyard too has a mission and accused him for not using it, so it was taken from him.

title.en: Seven notes, Shabbos and the song of matching

summary.en: The Rav explains the seven 'kolos' of Mizmor l'David in Kabbalas Shabbos as the seven notes of music, like the seven-stringed harp of the Beis HaMikdash, and the seven days of creation as seven notes completed by Shabbos and by David HaMelech. A chasunah reunites two matched halves of one soul, and music and poetry are also matching; so the kerem, the source of song and of matches, belonged to Navos, whose soul came from the root of David's song.

title.en: Why Achav wanted that vineyard

summary.en: The Rav explains that a person is drawn to what is his, citing the Satmar Rav's advice to follow one's inclination in a shidduch. Achav wanted Navos's vineyard because it held a part of his soul too, as shown by the fact that he inherited it, as in the Gemara's dispute on the property of those executed by the king. But he got it dishonestly, and the Zohar explains that his sin was not taking the vineyard, which a king may do, but the killing.

title.en: The vineyard that brought Achav to teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav asks how the vineyard helped Achav and answers that it brought him to teshuvah, since the gate of song is next to the gate of teshuvah, as a tzaddik explained the saying that a chazzan is a fool. He brings Rabbi Elazar on Achav's great teshuvah, notes that the miracle on Har HaKarmel did not move Achav while Eliyahu's rebuke over the vineyard did, and adds the Chovos HaLevavos that a sin which breaks a person's heart can be his good fortune.

title.en: Izevel's dancing and the root of song

summary.en: The Rav explains why Izevel was so eager for the vineyard and kept repeating 'Navos HaYizre'eli': she too came from the root of song, as in the Midrash the Tur brings that she would dance before every chassan and kallah, so her skull, hands and feet were not eaten by the dogs. Navos had failed his power of song, so she felt the vineyard was hers. The Rav concludes that whoever has bitachon will receive what is his without dishonesty.

title.en: Yehoyachin's food from the true King

summary.en: The Rav compares the verse in Yirmiyahu, that Yehoyachin's daily meals came 'from the king of Bavel', with the parallel verse in Melachim, which says only 'from the king'. Yirmiyahu is a sefer of hester panim, while Melachim reveals that the tzaddik Yehoyachin knew his food came from Hashem. He applies this to those who worry what any king can do, citing the Midrash that the same Achashverosh later brought joy to the Jews.

title.en: Elevating the sparks: the chair, the meal, the mission

summary.en: The Rav teaches that the whole redemption depends on elevating the sparks: a chair used for learning is elevated, one used for television sinks them deeper, and the roads to Tziyon mourn for lack of their tikkun. A meal is a guest that traveled from the field to a person's table, so he must wash, eat and bless with kavanah and recognize Hashem's kindness in the taste of food. He closes that from Beha'aloscha begins the period of travel and mission, and that Jews are Hashem's vineyard.

catalogTitle: קליפת נוגה יכול להתהפך לטוב; ענינים גשמיים יכולים להתהפך לטוב.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the body, food and worldly matters of a Jew, which come from klipas nogah, can be turned to holiness, while what comes from the three wholly impure klipos cannot.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the haftarah of Shavuos, where Yechezkel passes through four layers before the vision; the letter vav before 'nogah' marks it as a different kind of klipah, like the edible fourth peel of a nut. From the Tanya he explains that the body and animal soul of a gentile come from the three impure klipos, which cannot be elevated, while a Jew's body and kosher food come from nogah, which can; this is why only olos are accepted from gentiles. The inanimate world is not listed among the impure klipos because earth is batel to Hashem, as shown by the Girgashi and by Avraham's dust on erev Pesach. He then shows that the psak of the chachamim decides whether a thing falls into the impure klipos, and that even reality follows the Torah's psak. Finally, from Tanya ch. 7, he explains that eating, business, a joke or a vacation done for the sake of Heaven are raised to holiness.

en: Klipas nogah differs in kind from the three wholly impure klipos: what comes from it can be turned to good, while the three klipos cannot.
A gentile's body and animal soul come from the three impure klipos, so he can bring only an olah, while a Jew can eat meat for the sake of Heaven and bring shelamim.
The inanimate is not counted among the three impure klipos, because earth, the level of malchus, is batel to Hashem.
Whether something falls into the impure klipos depends on how the chachamim rule, and even physical reality follows the Torah's psak.
Permitted worldly acts such as eating, business or sleep become holiness when done for the sake of Heaven, and otherwise are no better than the animal soul itself.

title.en: The four klipos and the vav before nogah

summary.en: The Rav opens with Yechezkel's vision from the Shavuos haftarah and the four layers he passes through, compares them to the four peels of a nut, and explains that nogah alone can be turned to holiness. He shows this with the rule that only olos are accepted from gentiles, the Midrash about the chazir in the future, and the nesachim the Jews prepared from the meraglim's fruit.

title.en: Tanya ch. 6: the two levels of klipah

summary.en: The Rav compares nogah to the priah of a bris, which is not cut off but folded back, then reads the Tanya on the two levels of klipah. He explains that the souls of gentiles and forbidden foods from the inanimate, plants and animals come from the three impure klipos, while a Jew's body, kosher food and permitted matters like business and health come from nogah.

title.en: Why the inanimate is not in the impure klipos

summary.en: The Rav notes that the Tanya lists plants, animals and people among the three impure klipos but not the inanimate. He explains that the inanimate is malchus, earth, which is batel to Hashem, as Avraham called himself dust and ashes, and that the Girgashi, the nation opposite malchus, left the land on its own.

title.en: Avraham's dust against the kings on erev Pesach

summary.en: The Rav tells the Midrash that Og came to Avraham on erev Pesach while he baked matzos, and that Avraham fought the four kings into the night by throwing dust at them. He explains that dust is bitul, like bitul chametz, and this is how one nullifies the yetzer hara and the klipos.

title.en: The chacham's psak decides, and Reb Chaim Ozer's advice

summary.en: The Rav explains that when a question arises, Heaven rules as the chacham rules, so one should daven about it, as Dovid HaMelech did about his status. He tells how Reb Chaim Ozer advised a man with a lung illness to move to Eretz Yisroel, where the Beis Yosef's lenient ruling is followed, and he lived; every machlokes reflects different heavenly halls, and both views are true.

title.en: Reality follows the Torah's psak

summary.en: The Rav brings the mishnah in Niddah on the inner organs, where Rashi, Tosfos and the Rambam each describe the anatomy differently, and the Chasam Sofer's statement that reality matches the Rambam. He explains that the Torah is the blueprint of the world, each opinion has its place in Heaven, and since the halachah follows the Rambam, the anatomy follows him; he adds Rashi's comment on the missing yud in 'nesi'im'.

title.en: Nature changes with the chachamim's chiddushim

summary.en: The Rav explains that nature changes from generation to generation, with new illnesses and remedies, and brings Tosfos on a mishnah about the age at which a cow gives birth. Since nature follows the Torah's chiddushim, he explains why the Gemara sends one with a sick person to a chacham: a tzaddik cannot change the Torah, but a chacham can, through a chiddush, change the psak and with it the order of creation.

title.en: Tanya ch. 7: worldly acts for the sake of Heaven

summary.en: The Rav reads Tanya ch. 7 and explains that even eating kosher food, talking or doing business is nogah, which tips like a scale to holiness when done for the sake of Heaven, and otherwise is no better than the animal soul. He adds that in this world evil is the majority, from insects to people.

title.en: Good meat, wine and a joke before learning

summary.en: The Rav continues the Tanya: nogah is an intermediate level, and someone who eats fine meat and drinks wine to broaden his mind for Torah and mitzvos elevates them. Likewise a joke said to open the heart before learning, as Rabbah did before his students, is raised to holiness, unlike empty levity.

title.en: A vacation for the sake of Heaven

summary.en: Ending the season of Tanya, the Rav speaks about going to the country: seeing Hashem's natural world brings a person contentment and awareness of His greatness. A vacation taken to broaden the mind for avodah raises all of nature to holiness, and one taken otherwise drags it down to the impure klipos.

catalogTitle: לכל יהודי יש חלק בתורה מיוחד לו; טעם שמתוך שלא לשמה בא לשמה.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that every Jew has his own portion in the Torah and a hidden inner point of closeness to Hashem, and that this hidden point is why learning not for its own sake leads to learning lishmah.

abstract.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's definition of Torah lishmah: learning in order to bind one's soul to Hashem through grasping the Torah, each according to his intellect, and contrasts it with the Nefesh HaChaim's definition of learning to understand. Since every Jewish soul is rooted in the Torah, each person is drawn to particular parts of it. This leads him to the levels of pshat, remez, drush and sod, and to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who revealed the hidden part of the Torah. Every Jew, too, carries a sod: a hidden grace before Hashem that no one else knows. He illustrates this with Pesach Sheni, the people who were tamei who still asked why they should be left out, and their link to Nadav and Avihu, Pinchas and Lag BaOmer. Returning to the Tanya, he explains that a hidden point of lishmah lies within every act done not lishmah. He ends with the Tanya's teaching that Torah is food and garment, while mitzvos are garments alone.

en: According to the Tanya, learning Torah lishmah means learning in order to bind one's soul to Hashem through grasping the Torah, each according to his intellect.
Every Jewish soul is rooted in the Torah, so each person feels a desire for the particular part of the Torah where his soul is rooted.
Just as the Torah has pshat, remez, drush and sod, every Jew carries a sod: a hidden grace before Hashem that only Hashem knows.
The people who were tamei on Pesach Sheni could ask why they should be left out because their inner point is untouched by tumah, and in that hidden place all Jews are equal.
Learning not lishmah leads to lishmah because within every act not done lishmah lies a hidden point that wants to do it lishmah, and Hashem knows it.
Torah is food and also a garment for the soul, while mitzvos are only garments that surround a person from outside.

title.en: Lishmah and each soul's portion in Torah

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's definition of lishmah, binding the soul to Hashem through grasping the Torah, and contrasts it with the Nefesh HaChaim. He explains that every soul is rooted in the Torah, so each person is drawn to a particular part of it, and nowadays a person carries sparks of many souls whose desires change over the years.

title.en: The levels of Torah and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah has levels of pshat, remez, drush and sod, and that some souls belong to its inner part, the portion of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. Rashbi dug out and revealed the hidden part of the Torah, which will be the main learning when Moshiach comes, and this is the idea of Lag BaOmer.

title.en: Every Jew carries a secret

summary.en: Since every Jew is a letter in the Torah, he too has pshat, remez, drush and sod; his sod is a hidden grace before Hashem that no one else has, even when outwardly he looks like a sinner. The Rav brings the Chiddushei HaRim on this and the Beis Aharon that every Jew can find chizuk in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.

title.en: Chesed shebehod and the claim of Pesach Sheni

summary.en: The Rav notes that today is chesed shebehod, the start of the week of hod, which already carries the power of Lag BaOmer. He turns to the people who were tamei from a dead body and asked why they should be left out of the korban Pesach, and explains the halachos about who may not enter the camps.

title.en: Nadav and Avihu, Pinchas and Eliyahu

summary.en: The Rav explains that the people who were tamei had dealt with Nadav and Avihu, whose souls entered Pinchas, and Pinchas is Eliyahu. He asks why the passuk calls Pinchas the son of Elazar the son of Aharon HaKohen again, and answers that with Nadav and Avihu's souls he became also a son of Aharon.

title.en: The hidden point no tumah reaches

summary.en: The Rav explains that the people who were tamei received a spark of Nadav and Avihu's soul and so felt that in their inner point they were no different from other Jews. He ties Pesach Sheni, chesed shebehod, to Lag BaOmer, hod shebehod, and teaches that no Jew becomes so tamei that it takes hold of him entirely; in the sod all Jews are equal, like the circle dance of the tzaddikim.

title.en: Why not lishmah leads to lishmah

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Rav asks why learning not lishmah should lead to lishmah. He answers that Hashem knows that in his inner self every Jew wants to do it lishmah, so within every act done not lishmah lies a point of lishmah, and with this every Jew can bind himself to the Torah he learns.

title.en: Torah as food, mitzvos as garments

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya that Torah is food entering a person's inner self, while a mitzvah surrounds him like a garment. Most mitzvos relate to a particular limb, but tzitzis, sukkah and above all the spoken words of Torah surround the whole body, which is why Torah is also called a garment.

catalogTitle: תשובה על עבירות של שלש קליפות הטמאות' התיקון שבקריאת שמע בכוונה.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 7, the Rav explains why sins rooted in the three impure kelipos cannot be elevated except through teshuvah out of great love, and why the Ba'al HaTanya says the sin of wasted seed can be repaired through sincere teshuvah and krias shema al hamitah.

abstract.en: The Rav continues Tanya chapter 7. Permitted food eaten for pleasure rises again when the person returns to serving Hashem, though an impression stays in the body; forbidden things are bound by the kelipos until evil is uprooted in the days of Moshiach, as happened for one night at Yetzias Mitzrayim. Only teshuvah from the depth of the heart, with great love and longing, turns sins into merits and uproots them now. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar on bochurim spoiled by dishonest food, explains why a ba'al teshuvah stands higher than a tzaddik, tells of a former air-force pilot who became a ba'al teshuvah, and shows the same principle in the gedolim of Eretz Yisrael who came from abroad. Finally he explains the Ba'al HaTanya's chiddush that wasted seed, though the worst sin, is easier to repair, through krias shema al hamitah, and why the Torah does not state it as an explicit prohibition.

en: Permitted food eaten for pleasure rises again with the person when he returns to serving Hashem, but an impression of it stays in the body.
Forbidden things come from the three impure kelipos and stay bound there until evil is uprooted in the days of Moshiach.
Teshuvah from the depth of the heart, with great love and longing for Hashem, turns sins into merits and uproots evil even now.
A ba'al teshuvah, having been far from Hashem, thirsts for Him more than a tzaddik and rises with greater force.
Sins become merits because they were what brought the person to his teshuvah and to his higher level.
The life-force in wasted seed, though it falls into the three impure kelipos, can rise through sincere teshuvah and krias shema al hamitah with intense kavanah.

title.en: Permitted food rises, forbidden food stays bound

summary.en: The Rav reads Tanya chapter 7: permitted food eaten not for Heaven's sake rises again when the person returns to avodas Hashem, though an impression remains in the body, like a stain washed out of a garment. Forbidden things are bound by the three impure kelipos until their day comes, when Hashem slaughters the yetzer hara and death is swallowed up forever.

title.en: Yetzias Mitzrayim and teshuvah from love

summary.en: The Rav shows that evil was already nullified for one night at Yetzias Mitzrayim, bringing the Satmar Rav's answer on how korbanos could be taken from Egyptian animals. He then reads the Tanya that only a great teshuvah from the depth of the heart, turning sins into merits, can uproot evil from the impure kelipos now.

title.en: The Bnei Yissaschar: purifying a youth's path

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that good bochurim who later lose their desire for Torah were fed from money not earned honestly, and remarks how hard kashrus is to guard today. The remedy, from the passuk 'with all my heart I sought You', is teshuvah with the whole heart and a longing for Hashem, which draws a light of the future and can uproot even the three impure kelipos, especially at special times.

title.en: Why a ba'al teshuvah stands higher

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya that one who was far from Hashem thirsts for Him more than tzaddikim, and brings the Gemara that ba'alei teshuvah stand where tzaddikim cannot, with a mashal of a bird escaping a trap. He adds that before Moshiach all Jews will do teshuvah, and the present wave of teshuvah is the drizzle before the rain.

title.en: The pilot who became a ba'al teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav tells of a ba'al teshuvah who had been a leading pilot in the Israeli army and now learns all day, and who sat learning on Tisha B'Av night until kiddush levana rather than go home to eat. This, he says, is the extra force of ba'alei teshuvah, who draw a breath of the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Gedolim of Eretz Yisrael from abroad

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara 'one of us is like two of them' and shows it fulfilled: since the yishuv was renewed by the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Gra and the Chasam Sofer, nearly all the rabbanim and gedolim of Eretz Yisrael came from abroad. He explains that one who tears himself out of the darkness of galus comes with greater longing, which is the power of teshuvah.

title.en: How sins become merits

summary.en: The Rav explains that sins become merits because they caused the person's teshuvah and his higher level, and uses this to explain why one who says 'I will sin and repent' is not given the chance. Teshuvah not from love brings forgiveness and turns the sins into unintentional ones, but an impression remains and the sin stays in the kelipah until death is swallowed up forever.

title.en: Krias shema al hamitah repairs wasted seed

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya that the life-force in wasted seed can rise through sincere teshuvah and intense kavanah in krias shema al hamitah, as known from the Arizal and hinted in the Gemara. Though the Shulchan Aruch calls it the worst sin, it is easier to repair; he explains that the sitra achra forms bodies from the drops, and krias shema kills them and frees the holiness.

title.en: Why the Torah does not state it as a lav

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Torah mentions wasted seed only by hint, in the generation of the Flood and in Er and Onan, and answers from the Tanya that in this respect it is lighter than forbidden relations, since the life-force is not caught in a body. He contrasts the Zohar, read simply, with the Ba'al HaTanya, and explains that Hashem would not leave a Jew in a state with no way out, so the tzaddikim can give advice for its repair.

catalogTitle: תפילה: The Pleasure and Privilege of Attaching Oneself to Hashem

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the true purpose of tefillah is closeness and attachment to Hashem, a privilege and a pleasure beyond anything this world offers, and shows how to prepare for it and earn it.

abstract.en: The Rav describes tefillah as avodah shebalev that needs kavanah. Its goal is not to have a wish granted but dveikus, closeness to Hashem; asking even for small things, as Rav Nachum of Tchernobyl did for a maid, is complete emunah. Since a person is where his thoughts are, in davening he stands in the Beis HaMikdash, and unlike the angels and creatures of Perek Shirah, a Jew may sing to Hashem at any hour. Through the Kuzari, Rav Yonasan Eybeshitz and a Karlin story he shows that this sweetness surpasses every worldly pleasure. He urges preparation (ample time, slow words, a serious shul, mikveh, a pure mouth) and teaches that each word is an ark and a chamber in Gan Eden. He closes with Pesach Sheni and the week of Hod: self-nullification and love of every Jew, each a letter of the Torah with a hidden secret.

en: The Rav teaches that the goal of tefillah is not having one's wish fulfilled but closeness and attachment to Hashem.
Turning to Hashem in tefillah, even for small matters, is itself an act of emunah that He alone can do everything.
The Rav says the pleasure of a tefillah with kavanah surpasses every pleasure this world can give.
A good tefillah requires preparation: ample time, slow and attentive words, a serious shul and purity.
One must earn a good tefillah by overcoming the yetzer hara and guarding the mouth; a good davening without effort is only a free sample.
The week of Hod, which Pesach Sheni ushers in, calls for self-nullification and love of every Jew, since each Jew is a letter in the Torah with a hidden secret.

title.en: Closeness to Hashem and the mitzvah of tefillah

summary.en: The Rav opens with 'va'ani kirvas Elokim li tov' and says the Shechinah rests on ten Jews who gather to seek closeness to Hashem. He then explains that tefillah is avodah shebalev and must be said with kavanah, noting Chazal's requirement of kavanah in the first berachah of Shemoneh Esrei.

title.en: Tefillah as dveikus and emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains why today one does not repeat Shemoneh Esrei, since Hashem values the small avodah of our generation, and that tefillah with kavanah fulfills 'uvo sidbak'. Its aim is closeness to Hashem, not the granting of a wish, and turning to Hashem declares the emunah that He alone can provide everything.

title.en: The Tchernobyler Maggid prays for the maid

summary.en: The Rav tells how the talmidim of Rav Nachum of Tchernobyl overheard him asking Hashem that his Rebbetzin's maid should not quit, and how he answered that asking Hashem for small things is complete emunah. He adds that by davening a person declares that Hashem alone does everything.

title.en: An audience with the King; a person is where his thoughts are

summary.en: The Rav describes tefillah as the privilege of an audience with the King of kings, available at any moment. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's principle that a person is where his thoughts are, which the Avnei Nezer supports from the Gemara in Eruvin, so that when one davens facing the Beis HaMikdash he is truly there.

title.en: Hashem is near whenever we call; song at all hours

summary.en: From 'ki mi goy gadol' the Rav shows that Hashem is near whenever a Jew calls to Him, and that pouring out the heart is dveikus. He contrasts the angels, who sing once, and the creatures of Perek Shirah, who sing at set times, explaining tzafra and ramsha through the birds and creeping things, with the Jew who may sing to Hashem at any hour.

title.en: The sweetness of tefillah

summary.en: The Rav describes the sweetness of a tefillah with kavanah, bringing Yedid Nefesh, 'yismach lev mevakshei Hashem', the Kuzari on the times of tefillah as the fruit of one's day, and a passuk of David HaMelech. He then brings Rav Yonasan Eybeshitz's letter in Yaaros Devash, that despite ridicule for his long davening, standing in tefillah is the fruit of all his toil.

title.en: Preparing: time and slow words

summary.en: The Rav urges preparation for davening, above all setting aside ample time and not davening in twenty minutes. He brings the Magen Avraham's measure of a half hour for Pesukei Dezimra and the Rokeach's image of davening like one who counts silver coins.

title.en: Two stories of pleasure beyond the poritz

summary.en: The Rav tells the Karliner story of a poritz who spread sacks of sugar over a meadow to go sledding in August, and the Rebbe's answer that this cannot compare to his pleasure in saying Nishmas on Shabbos. He adds a story of Reb Moshe Leib of Sassov, who, fasting while trying to free captives, overcame a sudden hunger at the poritz's feast.

title.en: Why people belittle tefillah, and its purpose

summary.en: The Rav explains that the greater the mitzvah, the greater the yetzer hara against it, and brings the Gemara that tefillah stands at the heights of the world yet people belittle it. He says that in our sickly generation the emphasis must be on tefillah, and brings the Ramban that the purpose of all mitzvos and of creation is that people declare Hashem created them.

title.en: Each word of davening is an ark

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'tzohar ta'aseh lateivah': put light and one's whole being into each word of tefillah. He cites his Rebbe's explanation that this world is a flood in which people drown, and the word of davening is the ark that rescues a person and brings him to safe shores.

title.en: Aids to tefillah and the chambers of Gan Eden

summary.en: The Rav advises choosing a shul where davening is taken seriously, giving it time and thought, and using the mikveh, but says siyata dishmaya is still needed. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching, cited by the Chasam Sofer, that each word of davening is a chamber in Gan Eden from which one without kavanah is turned away, and the mashal of a storekeeper's free sample.

title.en: Killing the serpent to win the princess

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar's mashal of a serpent at the king's gate: whoever kills it wins the princess, who is tefillah, and the serpent is the yetzer hara. He adds that the mouth that davens must be pure from lashon hara, that a good davening may be the reward of a recent nisayon withstood, and the Arizal's instruction to accept love of one's fellow Jew before davening.

title.en: Pesach Sheni and the middah of Hod

summary.en: The Rav notes that the night is Pesach Sheni, entering the week of Hod in Sefirah, and explains Hod in plain terms as bittul, not being a 'yesh', personified by Aharon HaKohen, who rejoiced in his younger brother's greatness. He brings the Gemara linking Hod to the Beis HaMikdash, the place of bowing and self-nullification toward which we daven.

title.en: The talmidim of Rabbi Akiva and honor in a chavrusa

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hod means joining to Klal Yisrael, which erases one's faults, and brings the Beis Aharon that whoever believes in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai draws strength from him. He then reads the Gemara of Rabbi Akiva's twelve thousand pairs of talmidim, explaining that in each chavrusa the stronger one did not give honor to the weaker.

title.en: Every Jew is a letter of the Torah with a secret

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah, so even the smallest is indispensable, and each has a hidden secret, a sod, that others cannot see; Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai revealed the sod of the Torah, and then the talmidim stopped dying. He closes by urging chizuk in tefillah and ahavas Yisrael in the week of Hod, with a brachah for the final redemption.

catalogTitle: למצוא בדברי רשות נקודת אלקות' להשתמש בדברים גשמיים לשם שמים.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 7, the Rav explains that permitted worldly things come from kelipas nogah and that a Jew can raise them to holiness by using them for the sake of Heaven, as Yitzchak found living water in the wells he dug.

abstract.en: The Rav opens chapter 7 of Tanya: after showing that Torah and mitzvos clothe a person in holiness and sins clothe him in the sitra achra, the Alter Rebbe turns to permitted things. The animal soul of a Jew, kosher animals and permitted food come from kelipas nogah, a middle level that can tip either way. Eating, drinking and business are neutral in themselves; done for the sake of Heaven they rise to holiness, done for pleasure they fall to the kelipos. The world was created with the Torah, so every thing holds a point of G-dliness, and this is what Yitzchak's wells and Yaakov's sheep mean. Only a Jew can raise nogah. A plain person needs some pleasure, but with a measure each must judge for himself, as the Bnei Yissaschar explains. Pleasure taken for its own sake leaves a residue that needs chibut hakever, while forbidden things stay bound until the end of days.

en: The animal soul of a Jew comes from kelipas nogah, not from the three wholly impure kelipos, so the permitted things it uses can be turned to holiness.
A permitted thing is neutral in itself; whether it rises to holiness or falls to the kelipos depends on whether it is done for the sake of Heaven.
Since the world was created with the Torah, every thing in it holds a point of G-dliness, and a Jew came into the world to find it.
Only a Jew can raise kelipas nogah; for a non-Jew everything belongs to the three impure kelipos.
A plain person needs some pleasure from this world in order to learn and daven, but it must be taken with a measure that each one judges for himself.

Permitted food eaten for pleasure falls temporarily into the impure kelipos but can rise again when its strength is used for Torah and tefillah; its residue needs chibut hakever, while forbidden things stay bound until the end of days.

title.en: Permitted things and kelipas nogah

summary.en: The Rav recalls the previous chapter, where Torah and mitzvos clothe a person in holiness and sins in the sitra achra, and introduces chapter 7 on permitted things. The animal soul of a Jew is from kelipas nogah, so permitted things are neutral and depend on intent, which he shows with matzah, chametz and bread with butter.

title.en: The Tanya text: a middle level in a mostly evil world

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya: the vital soul of a Jew, kosher animals and permitted plants, and every permitted deed, word and thought not done for Heaven draw their life from kelipas nogah. He explains nogah as a middle level, like a scale that can tip either way, and shows that this world is mostly evil with a little good mixed in.

title.en: Yitzchak's wells: finding G-dliness in the earth

summary.en: The Rav applies the idea to eating and business done to serve Hashem, then turns to the parsha's account of Yitzchak's wells. Since the world was created with the Torah, the world is the composition and the Torah its commentary, and digging wells means finding the point of G-dliness in earthly things; he connects the three wells to weekday and Shabbos.

title.en: Yaakov's sheep and Yitzchak's blessing

summary.en: The Rav contrasts a modern biography with the Torah's account of Yaakov tending sheep for twenty years; only one who learns with emunah knows these were not plain dealings. Yitzchak's wells were dug for all of Klal Yisroel, and his blessing of dew, fat of the land, grain and wine shows the Avos could enter material things and raise the holy sparks in them.

title.en: Business for Heaven; only a Jew raises nogah

summary.en: Citing seforim on Noach and Vayetzei, the Rav says that business done in holiness, honestly and to have money for Torah, mitzvos and tzedakah, raises kelipas nogah and can reach great heights. Only a Jew can do this; he brings the Midrash that a non-Jew offers only olos, while a Jew can eat shelamim for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: A person needs pleasure, with a measure

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya on eating fat meat and drinking wine to broaden the mind for Hashem and His Torah, and explains that a plain person who is hungry cannot learn or daven. He tells of a psychologist's example of feeding through a zipper and of Rebbe Nachum of Chernobyl, and concludes that great tzaddikim aside, one must take pleasure with a measure.

title.en: Kedoshim tihyu, oneg Shabbos and Rabbah's joke

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar on kedoshim tihyu and the Ramban's 'naval birshus haTorah': the Torah cannot fix how much to eat because people differ, so each must judge for himself. He adds that on Shabbos the pleasure itself is the mitzvah, and explains Rabbah's joke before the shiur as bringing the students into a good mood so the joke was absorbed into holiness.

title.en: Pleasure for its own sake, chibut hakever and forbidden things

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya: one who eats only for pleasure brings the food's vitality down temporarily into the three impure kelipos, but because it was kosher it rises again when he learns and davens with its strength. The imprint of the pleasure remains and needs chibut hakever, while forbidden things stay bound to the kelipos until the end of days when death and impurity are removed.

catalogTitle: עליית שלש קליפות הטמאות - ע"י ביטול בששים' או תשובה מאהבה - זהו ניצוץ מימות המשיח. אין מציאות כתקלה עולמית.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that teshuvah out of love draws a flash of the days of Moshiach into a person's own world, which is why it can repair even what the Tanya calls beyond repair, and shows that Hashem never lets a sin become a mishap for the whole world.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews Tanya chapter 7: forbidden relations create a body and cannot be repaired except in the future or by great teshuvah out of love, which brings a flash of the days of Moshiach. He compares it to a lightning flash in the night and to Chanukah, when the light of Moshiach is revealed at the lighting. Hashem's domain is reshus hayachid and the klipah's is reshus harabim; Shabbos centers on hotza'ah, and Chanukah lights a candle in reshus harabim. Chanukah comes from Binah, the root of teshuvah out of love. He then explains why even such teshuvah cannot instantly repair a mamzer, and why a mamzer still dies through sustained teshuvah. Turning to Tanya chapter 8, he discusses forbidden food eaten unknowingly, the Tzemach Tzedek's link to the Rambam and the Mechaber, and why the Mishnah Berurah ruled like the Ra'avad: so that the cantonist children could still do teshuvah.

en: Following Tanya chapter 7, the Rav explains that forbidden relations cannot be repaired except in the future or by great teshuvah out of love, which already now draws a taste of the days of Moshiach.
Hashem's domain is reshus hayachid and the domain of the sitra achra is reshus harabim, which is why carrying out (hotza'ah) is the core of Shabbos.
Chanukah is a flash of the days of Moshiach in the darkness of exile, lighting a light in reshus harabim and turning Har Eisav into Har Tziyon.
Teshuvah out of love is Binah, the source of Chanukah, and one who does it lives the days of Moshiach in his own small world.
A mamzer cannot be repaired by a moment of teshuvah, but sustained teshuvah out of love can repair it, and then the mamzerim die; there is no situation in which a Jew's path to repair is closed.
The Rav explains that the Mishnah Berurah's ruling, that forbidden food eaten unknowingly can be elevated, was guided by Heaven so that the cantonist children could later do teshuvah.

title.en: Teshuvah out of love as a flash of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav reviews Tanya chapter 7: forbidden relations create a body and have no repair except in the future or by great teshuvah out of love, which brings a taste of the days of Moshiach. He compares this to a lightning flash in the night and to Chanukah, when, as the Bnei Yissaschar brings, the light of Moshiach is revealed at the lighting.

title.en: Reshus hayachid and reshus harabim

summary.en: The Rav asks what Chanukah and the days of Moshiach are, bringing the haftarah's verse that saviors will judge Har Eisav from Har Tziyon. He explains that Hashem's domain is reshus hayachid and the klipah's is reshus harabim, and shows from Maseches Shabbos and the verse 'let no man leave his place' that hotza'ah is the heart of Shabbos.

title.en: Kislev: lighting a candle in reshus harabim

summary.en: Kislev opens with Yaakov leaving the reshus hayachid of Eretz Yisrael for reshus harabim, and its avodah is to light a candle there, the light of Moshiach, until all becomes reshus hayachid in the day that is wholly Shabbos. He adds that the twenty-four days before Chanukah lead into it, as the sefarim count them against the letters of Baruch Shem and Shema Yisrael.

title.en: Binah, Chanukah and teshuvah out of love

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah comes from Binah, eight levels above Malchus, and that teshuvah out of love is Binah while teshuvah out of fear is Malchus. One who does teshuvah out of love brings the days of Moshiach into his own small world, and can therefore repair even forbidden relations and forbidden foods.

title.en: Why a mamzer needs sustained teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav explains why even teshuvah out of love cannot instantly repair a mamzer: the sin lives on in another body, a process the klipah dug into time. He brings the tradition that through great sustained teshuvah the mamzerim die, stresses that no Jew's path to repair is ever closed, and adds that Hashem also does not reveal families whose taint was forgotten.

title.en: Hashem's world cannot be ruined

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the nations' worry about pollution of air, water and the earth with the Jew's belief that Hashem created and runs the world and it cannot be ruined. A Jew's worry is to learn, daven, give tzedakah and have good middos; he brings the generation of the Tower, who worried about the heavens, against Avraham Avinu.

title.en: Forbidden foods and aveirah lishmah

summary.en: Returning to Tanya chapter 8, the Rav explains that forbidden foods are bound in the klipah, so even eaten unknowingly for the sake of Heaven they do not rise, and a true issur will be removed only in the days of Moshiach. He explains what an aveirah lishmah is, when it was permitted, and why eating forbidden food unknowingly is not one.

title.en: The Tzemach Tzedek, the Rambam and the Ra'avad

summary.en: The Rav brings the Tzemach Tzedek in Derech Mitzvosecha, who ties the Tanya's statement to the Rambam and the Mechaber, who rule that one who ate forbidden food unknowingly does not make a bracha acharonah, against the Ra'avad. Since a bracha elevates the food, no bracha means no elevation, while the Mishnah Berurah rules like the Ra'avad.

title.en: Why the Mishnah Berurah ruled otherwise

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Mishnah Berurah ruled differently and answers that nothing happens by chance: halachos follow each generation's sages, as with Rabbi Eliezer's view on preparations for milah and Beis Shammai's rulings in the days of Moshiach. In the Mishnah Berurah's time the Russian government forced thousands of cantonist children to eat forbidden food, and Heaven guided his ruling so that they could still do teshuvah.

catalogTitle: עונשים -על הנאה גשמיות' לעם הארץ שמבטל תורה' לתלמיד חכם המבטל תורה; לימוד חכמת חיצוניות יותר חמור מדברים בטלים.

oneLiner.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 8, the Rav explains the lasting imprint of physical pleasure and idle talk, the special severity of bitul Torah for one who can learn, and why secular wisdom studied for its own sake is worse than idle talk, permitted only as a means for the sake of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Rav continues Tanya chapter 8. Forbidden food comes from the three impure kelipos, and even a rabbinic prohibition rests on the food itself. Kosher food eaten for pleasure falls temporarily into kelipas noga; even if later elevated, an imprint remains in the body, like a stain that survives washing, and only chibut hakever removes it, unless one, like Rebbi, never enjoyed this world. Idle talk of an am ha'aretz is kelipas noga, cleansed by kaf hakela; a talmid chacham who could learn commits bitul Torah, with its own severe punishment, beyond the cold Gehinom for neglected positive mitzvos. Secular wisdom is worse than idle talk: idle talk comes from the middos, as animals chatter, while wisdom comes from chabad that fell into kelipah at the breaking of the vessels. It is allowed only as a means, for parnassah or serving Hashem, with honest calculations and never through studies bound up with heresy and sin.

en: Kosher food eaten for pleasure falls into kelipas noga, and even after it is elevated an imprint remains in the body that only chibut hakever removes.
Idle talk of one who cannot learn is kelipas noga, while for a talmid chacham who could learn it is the sin of bitul Torah, with its own severe punishment.
Studying secular wisdom when one could learn Torah is worse than idle talk, because it clothes the soul's chabad in kelipah.
Secular wisdom reached the nations through the breaking of the vessels, when chochmah fell into the kelipos.
Torah must be learned for its own sake, while secular wisdom may be learned only as a means, for parnassah or to serve Hashem.
The permission has two conditions: the intent must be for the sake of Heaven, and the studies may not be bound up with prohibitions such as heresy.

title.en: Forbidden food and the impure kelipos

summary.en: The Rav reads Tanya on forbidden food, which cannot be elevated, and mentions the Tzemach Tzedek's notes on rabbinic prohibitions, explaining that even a rabbinic prohibition rests on the food itself. He contrasts the desire for forbidden things, from the gentile 'demons' of the impure kelipos, with the desire for kosher things, which can be elevated.

title.en: The imprint of permitted pleasure

summary.en: The Rav explains that kosher food eaten for pleasure enters kelipas noga and leaves an imprint in the body even after teshuvah, like a stain that survives washing, removed only by chibut hakever. He brings Rebbi, who raised his ten fingers and said he had not enjoyed this world, though he was very wealthy, as Rashi in Toldos shows.

title.en: Idle talk: the am ha'aretz and the talmid chacham

summary.en: The Rav explains that the idle talk of an am ha'aretz who cannot learn is not itself a sin, but is kelipas noga and needs cleansing by kaf hakela. A talmid chacham who could learn commits bitul Torah, and the Rav explains the fire Gehinom for active sins, the snow Gehinom for neglected positive mitzvos, and a special punishment for bitul Torah.

title.en: Secular wisdom counts as idle talk

summary.en: The Rav reads Tanya that the wisdom of the nations is included in idle talk regarding bitul Torah, and is worse. Mathematics or physics studied when one could learn is idle talk compared to Torah. He brings Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya to show that the wisdom of the nations rises and falls opposite the sages of Torah.

title.en: Earlier generations' depth, today's details

summary.en: In a digression the Rav observes that recent generations developed pilpul and new chiddushim, while the earlier Rishonim had deeper knowledge; likewise the nations' earlier wise men pursued wisdom for its own sake, while today's science is details and machinery. A doctor once knew a patient's state from his face and pulse; today it is tests and electronics.

title.en: Idle talk from the middos, wisdom from chabad

summary.en: The Rav explains that empty chatter comes from the middos, as animals bark and sing, while wisdom comes from chabad, and kelipah too has chabad. So one who studies secular wisdom to be a scientist when he could learn does greater damage than one who tells jokes, since the impurity reaches the soul's chabad. He then rereads the Tanya's words on this.

title.en: The breaking of the vessels

summary.en: The Rav brings the beginning of Tanya chapter 3: the seven middos have good and evil, while chabad is only good. He explains, calling it an awesome matter, that at the breaking of the vessels chochmah fell into the kelipos, which is why the nations have wisdom, and why engaging in it gives the kelipah a hold on something from a very high place.

title.en: Torah lishmah, secular wisdom only as a means

summary.en: The Rav explains the exception: one who studies secular wisdom for parnassah, to support his family in Torah and to learn, elevates it like eating for the sake of Heaven. Torah must be learned lishmah and never as a spade, as the Mishnah says, while secular wisdom must be learned as a spade, not for its own sake; a better-paying profession can leave more time to learn.

title.en: All wisdom is found in the Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains the reason of the Rambam and Ramban for studying these wisdoms: to serve Hashem, such as drawing people closer to Torah. He adds that they knew the wisdoms from the Torah itself, citing the Ramban's introduction to Chumash, and points to tzaddikim whom doctors consulted and Rebbes who wrote prescriptions without schooling, since one who learns lishmah knows everything.

title.en: Honest calculations and the two conditions

summary.en: The Rav warns that the intent must be honest: few who study medicine do so for chessed, and many calculations about parnassah are false. An aveirah cannot be done lishmah, so college, where one must study heresy and faces tests of immorality, has no heter even for parnassah. He concludes with two conditions: intent for the sake of Heaven and studies free of prohibitions.

catalogTitle: אמונה: Having אמונה throughout עקבתא דמשחא When 'ה Seems Distant

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha faces the test of the Akeidah, holding on to emunah when Hashem seems distant and the questions seem unanswerable.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah's description of ikvesa d'Meshicha, the 'heel' of history, and shows its signs in his own day: brazenness, places of gathering turned into centers of immorality, and the theater and television that now enter the home. The heel is insensitive and in the dark, yet it carries the whole body, so everything depends on this generation. He then turns to the Akeidah: a nisayon is a test meant to raise a person, and the tenth test should be the hardest, yet being thrown into the fire at Ur Kasdim seems harder. He answers from 'vayar es hamakom merachok': at the Akeidah Hashem seemed distant, and the command seemed to contradict His promise about Yitzchak, but Avraham did not argue and held on to his emunah. Following the Ramban that the deeds of the Avos foreshadow their children, the Rav concludes that the last generation faces this same test, and that those who hold on to emunah will merit the blessing given to Avraham.

en: History is built like a human body from head to heel, and the Rav says tzaddikim have stated that this generation is the heel, ikvesa d'Meshicha.
The heel is the most insensitive and darkest part of the body, yet the whole body stands on it, so the whole history of Klal Yisrael depends on how the last generation behaves.
A nisayon means both a test and a raising, because the purpose of a test is to promote the one who passes it.
The Akeidah was the hardest of Avraham's tests because Hashem, who had been close to him, now seemed distant, and the command seemed to contradict His promise about Yitzchak.
Avraham did not argue with Hashem; he held on to his emunah without understanding, and went to the Akeidah with a heavy heart.
Following the Ramban that what happened to the Avos is a sign for their children, the Akeidah foreshadows the last test of Klal Yisrael before the Geulah.
The Rav says the mitzvah of this generation is emunah: to believe without seeing, though Hashem seems distant.
