title.en: Our generation as the heel of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah that in ikvesa d'Meshicha brazenness will increase, explains that Jewish history is built like a body from head to heel, and says that tzaddikim have identified this generation as the heel.

title.en: The signs of the time: gatherings, theater, television

summary.en: The Rav reads further in the Mishnah that the places of gathering will become places of immorality, and shows how the theater and television, which once had to be visited, now enter the home. He brings Ruth's words to Naomi and the breakdown of respect for elders, and asks how a Jew can survive this period.

title.en: The heel: insensitive, dark, and carrying everything

summary.en: The Rav explains that the heel feels almost no pain and is always in the dark, like a generation insensitive to its heritage; yet the whole body stands on the heel, so the few who are not swept away support the entire structure of the generations before them.

title.en: The Akeidah: a nisayon is a raising

summary.en: The Rav turns to the parshah of the Akeidah said every day and asks what its message is. He explains that the root of nisa means both to test and to raise, like a banner, because the purpose of a test is to promote the student who passes it.

title.en: The tenth test seems easier than Ur Kasdim

summary.en: The Rav argues that the tenth test should be the hardest, since everything depended on it, yet the first test seems harder: Avraham let himself be thrown into the fire by Nimrod for a G-d he had never seen. Only after he came out of the fire did Hashem first speak to him, as in the Midrash's parable of the owner of the building.

title.en: He saw the place from afar: Hashem seemed distant

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Akeidah was the hardest test and answers from 'vayar es hamakom merachok': Hashem, who had been intimate with Avraham, now seemed far. He compares this to the times every servant of Hashem loses his desire to learn and daven, often out of disappointment, and shows how the command about Yitzchak seemed to contradict Hashem's promise.

title.en: Avraham does not argue; the simple answer he could not see

summary.en: The Rav describes how Avraham, with a question in his heart, did not argue with Hashem or listen to the Satan, but went to the Akeidah with a heavy heart and perfect emunah. He then notes that the question has a simple answer, given by Rashi and the angel, that Hashem only said to bring Yitzchak up, and explains that in the time of a test one cannot see the answer.

title.en: The Ramban: the Avos foreshadow their children

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban at the beginning of Lech Lecha that the lives of the Avos were a sign of what would happen to their children, with the examples of the famine, Egypt and Pharaoh. From this he concludes that the Akeidah, Avraham's last and hardest test, foreshadows the last test of Klal Yisrael, which is happening now.

title.en: The test of our generation: emunah without seeing

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the questions raised after the destruction of European Jewry, in books asking where G-d was, and says this generation lives in a time when Hashem seems distant. Its mitzvah is emunah, believing without seeing, and the theater, television, newspapers and books are agents of the Satan like the one who tried to stop Avraham.

title.en: The blessing of 'eikev asher shamata'

summary.en: The Rav concludes that Avraham received the angel's blessing 'eikev asher shamata' because he listened in a time of distance, and that the Geulah depends on this generation passing the test of the Akeidah. He says fortunate is the one who holds on to emunah, and that when the Geulah comes all the questions will be answered so simply that people will wonder how they did not see it.

catalogTitle: התחלת התשובה' על דרך עבודה' לתרץ הקושיות שבראש הספר. רשע ורע לו צדיק ורע לו (הרע כפוף בו) צדיק וטוב לו מהותם.

oneLiner.en: Opening Tanya chapter 10, the Rav explains the tzaddik gamur, who has turned his evil into good and hates this world's pleasures out of love of Hashem, the tzaddik she'eino gamur, whose evil is only subdued, and the bnei aliyah who raise the evil up and serve Hashem for the sake of the Shechinah.

abstract.en: The Rav explains that until chapter 10 the Tanya laid down foundations; now the path of avodah begins, and the questions of chapter one on tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo will be answered. The tzaddik gamur and the rasha gamur are two extremes that have lost their bechirah: one has turned his evil into good, the other, like Pharaoh, his good into evil. He tells of tzaddikim who remembered earlier gilgulim. The tzaddik gamur hates this world's pleasures because they come from the sitra achra and are the opposite of his love of Hashem with delight, illustrated by stories of the Beis Aharon and the Berditchever. The tzaddik she'eino gamur hates evil only according to his level; his evil is subdued and nullified, not transformed. Finally he explains the bnei aliyah, who raise the evil up to holiness and serve Hashem for a need on High, to do kindness with the Shechinah in exile.

en: From chapter 10 the Tanya moves from foundations to the path of avodah and begins answering the questions of chapter one.
The tzaddik gamur has transformed his evil into good, while the rasha gamur has transformed his good into evil; both extremes no longer have real bechirah.
The tzaddik gamur hates the pleasures of this world because they come from the kelipah, the opposite of his love of Hashem with delight.
In the tzaddik she'eino gamur the evil is subdued and nullified by the good, but it remains evil, so he is called tzaddik v'ra lo.
Hatred of evil and love of Hashem go together: only one who hates evil completely can love Hashem completely.
The bnei aliyah raise the evil up to holiness, and they serve Hashem not to quench their own thirst for Him but to do kindness with the Shechinah in exile.

title.en: From foundations to the path of avodah

summary.en: The Rav explains that until chapter 10 the Tanya laid down foundations, and from here the path of avodah begins and the questions of chapter one are answered. He reads the opening of the chapter and sets out the two extremes: the tzaddik gamur who has turned his yetzer hara into good, and the rasha who has turned his good into evil.

title.en: Pharaoh, and tzaddikim without bechirah

summary.en: Using Pharaoh, whose heart was turned to evil, the Rav shows that the two extremes have lost their bechirah. He tells of tzaddikim such as the Yismach Moshe and the Apter Rav who remembered their earlier gilgulim, and explains that Pharaoh let the Jews go not by free choice; until Matan Torah, he adds, non-Jews could still reach a high level, as the Ramchal discusses.

title.en: Tzaddik v'ra lo and tzaddik v'tov lo

summary.en: After placing the beinoni between the extremes, the Rav reads the Tanya: one who drives out evil but has not transformed it is a tzaddik she'eino gamur, tzaddik v'ra lo, whose evil is only bent and suppressed. The tzaddik gamur has turned it fully to good, has removed the soiled garments, and despises the pleasures of this world.

title.en: Love of Hashem with delight

summary.en: The Rav explains why the tzaddik gamur hates this world's pleasures: they come from the kelipah, while he serves Hashem with a love full of delight. He brings the Beis Aharon on the word 'kamah', his reply about a nobleman who went sledding on sugar in summer, a tzaddik who could not tear himself away from Shemoneh Esrei, and the Berditchever who rushed to learn Gemara Sukkah after Yom Kippur; the measure of the love is the measure of the hatred of the sitra achra.

title.en: Why we must know what a tzaddik is

summary.en: The Rav asks why people who are not tzaddikim need to know this, and answers that one must love tzaddikim and know whose Torah one learns. The tzaddik she'eino gamur hates this world only according to his level, which he illustrates with the countless levels among people; one should not be shaken by still feeling an attraction to this world, since fighting it is our avodah. He returns to the tzaddikim who remembered earlier gilgulim and explains why others are not given that memory.

title.en: Evil nullified, and the levels of tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the tzaddik she'eino gamur the evil is nullified by the strength of the good so that he never sins, yet it remains evil, and so he is tzaddik v'ra lo; one who does not hate evil completely does not love Hashem completely, except at high moments. This level divides into countless levels, from those whose evil is batel b'shishim, which he connects with the Gemara's numbers of 18,000, 36 and one tzaddik.

title.en: The bnei aliyah

summary.en: The Rav explains why the true tzaddikim gemurim are called bnei aliyah: they raise the evil up to holiness, as in the Zohar's story of R' Chiya at the heichal of R' Shimon bar Yochai, where darkness is turned to light. A second reason is that they serve Hashem for a need on High, not even to quench their own thirst for Him, but to do kindness with the Shechinah in exile, as the Tikkunim and the Ra'aya Mehemna describe.

catalogTitle: מלחמת יצה"ר ויצה"ט על העיר הקטנה. שניהם רוצים שהשני יהיה בטל אצלו.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains how the Godly soul and the animal soul fight like two kings over the 'small city' of the body, each wanting the other to be subdued to it, and what this war asks of an ordinary person.

abstract.en: Learning Tanya chapter 9, the Rav explains that the animal soul of a Jew, from kelipas nogah, dwells in the blood-filled left chamber of the heart, while the Godly soul dwells in the brain and the right chamber. The heart's blood even drives the brain to scheme for the heart's desires; the liver, all blood, is lower still, and a Midrash reads Pharaoh's 'heavy heart' as a heart that was really a liver. Contemplation of Hashem's greatness gives birth to love, as Birchas Yotzer leads to Ahavah Rabbah. The body is a small city over which the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara wage constant war, each wanting the other subdued. The yetzer tov wants its love to overflow into the left chamber until even appetite serves Hashem, as with matzah eaten with appetite. Only a tzaddik gamur transforms his evil; for most people the avodah is to subdue it, and the Zohar's parable shows the yetzer hara itself serves the King.

en: The animal soul dwells in the blood-filled left chamber of the heart, and the Godly soul dwells in the brain and spreads to the right chamber, where there is hardly any blood.
The desires of the heart rise to the brain and drive it to scheme how to fulfil them, because the heart sends its blood to the brain.
The body is a small city over which the Godly soul and the animal soul wage a lifelong war, each wanting the whole body subjugated to it alone.
The yetzer tov wants the love born of contemplation to fill the right chamber and overflow into the left, so that even the bad inclinations are subdued and used for good.
Only a tzaddik gamur transforms his yetzer hara into good; for the vast majority of people the avodah is to subdue it, like a king who imprisons the enemy king.
The yetzer hara itself is there for a person's good: like the harlot in the Zohar's parable, its true wish is that the person withstand it.

title.en: The animal soul in the left chamber of the heart

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's words that the animal soul of a Jew, from kelipas nogah, dwells in the blood-filled left chamber of the heart. He explains the two chambers, the blood as the vehicle of the vital soul, and why a Jew's animal soul can be transformed to good.

title.en: Desires rise to the brain; the Godly soul's seat

summary.en: The Rav explains how the desires of the heart spread through the body and rise to the brain, which plans how to fulfil them because the heart's blood drives it. He then reads that the Godly soul dwells in the brain and in the right chamber, 'the heart of the wise is on his right'.

title.en: The liver, and Pharaoh's heart

summary.en: The Rav explains that the liver, lower than heart and brain, is full of blood, which is why the poskim say it cannot be salted but must be roasted. He tells the Midrash of the lion, the donkey that had 'no heart' and the fox, and the Midrash's reading of 'Pharaoh's heart is heavy' as a heart that was a liver.

title.en: The heart of the wise is on his right

summary.en: The Rav explains that good middos come from the right chamber and bad ones from the left, and that the wise man's contemplation of Hashem's greatness arouses love of Hashem in the right chamber. He shows this in the order of tefillah, where Birchas Yotzer's contemplation gives birth to the love of Ahavah Rabbah.

title.en: Two kings fighting over the small city

summary.en: The Rav brings 'one nation shall overpower the other' about Yaakov and Esav as the constant war of the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara, and the Tanya's image of the body as a small city two kings fight over. He explains that the Godly soul wants to rule the body alone, with all its limbs, powers and garments subjugated to it.

title.en: Chabad gives birth to love that overflows

summary.en: The Rav explains what the yetzer tov wants: chochmah, binah and daas of the Godly soul filling the mind, giving birth to fear and love like a father and mother give birth to children. The love is to fill the right chamber until it spills into the left and subdues the sitra achra there.

title.en: Matzah with appetite: serving with both inclinations

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Mishnah wants matzah eaten with appetite if a mitzvah should be done only for Hashem's will, and answers that the yetzer hara must serve the yetzer tov. The appetite gives the mitzvah its fire, and this is 'with all your heart, with both your inclinations'.

title.en: Love with delight and avodas matanah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the yetzer tov wants the 'evil waters', the drive for pleasure, transformed into love of Hashem, up to love with delight that even simple people taste at high moments such as Shabbos. He distinguishes 'avodas avodah', service by toil, from 'avodas matanah', service as a gift.

title.en: Not a tzaddik gamur; the Zohar's parable

summary.en: Anticipating the next chapter, the Rav explains that only a tzaddik gamur transforms his yetzer hara, while most people's avodah is to subdue it, so no one should despair. He finishes the chapter: the yetzer tov wants thought, speech and action for Hashem alone, the animal soul wants the opposite, yet it too serves man's good, as the Zohar's parable of the king's son and the harlot shows.

catalogTitle: אמונה: Having בטחון in these Days of Fear

oneLiner.en: Speaking impromptu at a time of fear of war, the Rav explains that before Moshiach Hashem hides Himself as in the Megillah, that the birth pains of Moshiach can pass as fear alone, and that the response is bitachon together with Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

abstract.en: Asked to speak about current events, the Rav opens with the birth pains of Moshiach and shows from the 400 years of Mitzrayim, cut short to 210, that the decreed suffering need not come in full; it can be discharged through fear alone. He explains the double concealment, hester panim within hester panim, foretold for the end of days, with a parable of a father hidden from his son. He ties the looming war with Iraq to the troubles from Yishmael, then teaches that Adar, the end of the year, mirrors the end of time: its miracles, like those of the Megillah, are hidden inside ordinary events, and today's news is likewise a Megillah being written. Yishmael, a 'pere adam', is spreading fear, and the answer is the mitzvah of bitachon, which breaks the concealment. He tells stories of bitachon, urges Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, notes the lack of great leaders today, and ends with Az Yashir and the joy of Adar.

en: The birth pains of Moshiach need not come in full; just as the 400 years of Mitzrayim became 210, Klal Yisrael can be discharged through fear alone.
Before Moshiach there is a double concealment: not only is Hashem hidden, but the very fact that He is hidden is hidden.
Adar, the end of the year, mirrors the end of time: its miracles are hidden in natural events, as in the Megillah, where Hashem's name does not appear.
Everything happening in the world today, whatever the leaders say or plan, is part of a Megillah that Hashem is writing for the Jews.
Bitachon is a mitzvah, and a person who tells Hashem that he relies on Him sees Hashem's care and breaks through the hester panim.
Real bitachon is the work of a lifetime, but whoever has not yet worked on it should start now, together with tefillah, Torah and tzedakah.

Torah, tefillah and tzedakah as protection

title.en: Birth pains of Moshiach need not come in full

summary.en: The Rav explains that he was asked minutes earlier to speak about current events and must rely on Hashem for the words. He describes the coming of Moshiach as a birth accompanied by pains, then proves from the 400 years of Mitzrayim that lasted only 210 that the foretold suffering need not come in full.

title.en: Fear instead of suffering; hester within hester

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rebbe Reb Elimelech, who said he had nullified the birth pains of Moshiach, and tzaddikim who said the Holocaust was not yet those pains, and teaches that one can be discharged through fear. He then explains the double hiding of Hashem foretold in Vayelech with a parable of a hunter's son who does not even know his father is near.

title.en: The war with Iraq and the trouble from Yishmael

summary.en: The Rav connects the looming war with Iraq to Chazal's words that before Moshiach the Jews will have trouble from Yishmael. He reviews the four kingdoms, from Bavel to Edom, Hashem's coming revenge from the end of Haazinu, and the Midrashim and the Rambam that call Yishmael the worst, then returns to fear at the end of time.

title.en: Nisan and Adar; today's events as a Megillah

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Nisan, the month of revealed miracles, with Adar, when miracles are cloaked in a chain of small events, as in the Megillah, which has no name of Hashem. He explains that Achashverosh alludes to Hashem, pictures yeshiva boys rejecting gossip about Vashti that became part of the Megillah, and concludes that today's world events are also part of a Megillah.

title.en: The fear from Yishmael and the mitzvah of bitachon

summary.en: The Rav says that, as in the Megillah where Haman's decree produced only fear, today's fear comes from Yishmael, a 'pere adam' who cannot be reasoned with. Against it he sets the mitzvah of bitachon from the first of the Ten Commandments, explaining that one who tells Hashem he relies on Him breaks the hester panim.

title.en: Living with bitachon now: stories and protection

summary.en: The Rav says the call of the hour is not to be frightened but to trust Hashem like a child hiding under its mother's apron. He tells of the Steipler during the Gulf War and of a soldier saved by saying Shema, recalls how Hashem helped the Jews in the wars since the Holocaust, and urges davening, learning and tzedakah as protection.

title.en: No leaders to rely on; Az Yashir and Adar

summary.en: The Rav explains that before Moshiach the Jews will have no great leaders to rely on, as is the situation today, so they must rely on Hashem alone. He brings a Midrash that all salvations are in Az Yashir, asks that the fear fall on the nations like Haman's decree turned on Haman, and closes with the Gemara on Adar and a call to be joyful and not afraid.

catalogTitle: רשע וטוב לו' הטוב כפוף בו' רבבות מדריגות בו. רשע ורע לו. בינוני' הרע בו כמו הטוב אבל הוא אינו עושה רע. ובעיתות 'רצון' הרע הולך לו.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapters 11 and 12, the Rav explains the levels of the rasha v'tov lo and the rasha v'ra lo, and defines the beinoni as one who never sins, whose evil is silenced during proper davening.

abstract.en: The Rav opens chapter 11 of Tanya: opposite the tzaddik v'ra lo stands the rasha v'tov lo, whose good is bent under the evil in countless levels; the lightest stumbles only rarely, in a little lashon hara, levity or a sinful thought. He explains why hirhurei aveirah are easy to fall into yet graver than a deed, since thought reaches the world of Beriah. He discusses when thought alone is a sin, the rasha who regrets and the three kinds of atonement, and then the rasha v'ra lo, from whom the good has departed yet still surrounds him as a makif, so that he may complete a minyan. In chapter 12 he defines the beinoni as one who never sins though he still has free choice, notes that every Jew can become a beinoni, and explains that during krias shema and tefillah the evil in him is silenced, while afterward it may speak but he does not listen.

en: The rasha v'tov lo still has good within him, but it is bent and suppressed under the evil, and there are countless levels of how much it is suppressed.
Sinful thoughts are light in that even upright people easily stumble in them, but graver than a sin in their damage, since a bad thought blemishes the world of Beriah.
The rasha v'ra lo has driven the good out of himself and never does teshuvah, yet the good still surrounds him as a makif, so he remains a Jew who believes and can complete a minyan.
A beinoni never commits a sin, yet unlike the complete tzaddik he still has free choice; the Tanya, the 'Sefer shel Beinonim', teaches how to be a beinoni, which every Jew can become.
During krias shema and tefillah said properly, the evil in the beinoni is silenced and only the yetzer tov rules; after davening the evil may speak again, but the beinoni does not listen to it.

title.en: The rasha v'tov lo and his levels

summary.en: Recalling the tzaddik v'ra lo of the previous chapter, the Rav reads the opening of chapter 11: the rasha v'tov lo, whose good is bent under the evil in countless levels. The lightest of them falls rarely, in one of the three garments: a little lashon hara or levity in speech, or sinful thoughts.

title.en: Why sinful thoughts are light yet severe

summary.en: The Rav describes the 'light' rasha who has not yet done teshuvah, and explains the two sides of hirhurei aveirah: they are easy to fall into, even for upright people, yet worse than a sin. He maps action, speech and thought onto the worlds of Asiyah, Yetzirah and Beriah, so a bad thought blemishes as high as the Throne of Glory.

title.en: When thought alone is a sin; regret and atonement

summary.en: The Rav explains that a bad thought is generally not joined to the deed, except in heresy and immorality, where the thought itself is the sin. Even an upright Jew who stumbles in such things is called a rasha at that moment, but afterward the good in him regrets and he seeks forgiveness; the Rav lists the three kinds of atonement.

title.en: The rasha v'ra lo: the good surrounds him

summary.en: The Rav moves to one who often falls into grave sins yet still has regrets, still a rasha v'tov lo, and then to the rasha v'ra lo, who never does teshuvah because the good has departed from within him. Even so he believes in the Ribono shel Olam and would give his life rather than serve idols, because the good stands around him as a makif, as if waiting at the door.

title.en: Counting him for a minyan

summary.en: As an example the Rav explains that such a person may be counted for a minyan, and explains what a minyan is: ten souls join into one and draw down a holiness that nine tzaddikim cannot. He asks how one whose good has left can join, answers that the kedushah stays around him as a makif, and reads the closing lines of chapter 11 with the saying that wherever ten are gathered the Shechinah rests.

title.en: Who is a beinoni

summary.en: Opening chapter 12, the Rav defines the beinoni as one who never sins yet still has free choice, which answers how Rabbah could think he was a beinoni. He notes the title 'Sefer shel Beinonim': the Ba'al HaTanya cannot make anyone a tzaddik, but every Jew can become a beinoni. 'Never sinned and never will' refers to his present state, as even great people like the meraglim and Korach fell.

title.en: Krias shema and tefillah as a time of gadlus

summary.en: The Rav explains that the ten powers of the beinoni's G-dly soul do not rule alone, yet at special times the evil has no say: during krias shema and tefillah, a time of gadlus hamochin when a Jew rises to higher worlds where there is no evil. Then he awakens the love of Hashem in the right chamber of his heart and fulfills the mitzvah of loving Hashem.

title.en: Preparing to daven; the two judges

summary.en: The Rav walks through the preparation from waking up through pesukei dezimra, birchas yotzer, ahavah rabbah and shema, which brings a time when the yetzer hara is silenced. He compares the beinoni to a court with two judges who listens only to the good one, and stresses that this is only with proper davening, not a rushed one; after davening the evil may speak again, but the beinoni does not heed it.

catalogTitle: בינוני מוח שליט על הלב' היצה"ר אינו מתלבש בלבוש מחשבה דיבור או מעשה אבל הוא במציאות אצלו.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 12, the Rav explains that in the beinoni the evil inclination is still present but can never clothe itself in thought, speech or deed, because the mind rules over the heart.

abstract.en: The Rav recalls the question from chapter one, how Rabbah could call himself a beinoni, and how the earlier chapters defined the tzaddik; the beinoni never sins yet still desires evil, so in essence he is not called a tzaddik. Chapter 12 explains that his evil never gains enough strength to clothe itself in his body; he may even have once been wicked and done teshuvah. Using the Tanya's parable of two kings fighting over a small city, the Rav explains the exception of Shema and tefillah, and expands on davening as passage through the heavenly chambers, where foreign thoughts mean being pushed out, and on preparing with teshuvah and joining oneself to all Jews. The evil inclination stays a mere passer-by, never a guest or master, because the mind rules the heart. He adds that rare situations can exist where a person truly cannot help himself, but one must always suspect that he can. A bad thought is driven out by holy thoughts, as light drives away darkness. Finally, even after davening the yetzer suggests things, and the impression of davening and the hidden love keep the beinoni in control.

en: The beinoni never sins, but because he still has a desire for evil he is not called a tzaddik in essence, only in judgment.
In the beinoni the evil never becomes strong enough to clothe itself in the body through thought, speech or deed.
During Shema and tefillah, when the mind is in a state of greatness, the evil in the beinoni has no dominion at all; afterwards it reawakens.
The mind rules over the heart by the nature of man's creation, so a person can always overcome his yetzer and cannot claim he was unable to help it.
A bad thought is best driven away by thinking of holy matters, just as a little light drives away much darkness.
Even after davening the yetzer still sits in its place and makes suggestions; the impression of the davening and the hidden love keep the beinoni in control.

title.en: Rabbah's question and the tzaddik defined

summary.en: The Rav recalls the question from chapter one, how Rabbah, who served Hashem every moment, could call himself a beinoni, and reviews the complete tzaddik who has killed his evil inclination. He explains that the beinoni never sins, yet since he still desires evil he is a tzaddik only in judgment, not in essence.

title.en: The evil cannot clothe itself in the body

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of Tanya chapter 12: in the beinoni the evil never gains enough strength to clothe itself in thought, speech or deed. He adds that one may become a beinoni after teshuvah, and recalls the parable of two kings fighting over a small city, where the good king holds his position, except during Shema and tefillah.

title.en: Davening as passage through the heichalos

summary.en: The Rav explains, in the name of the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Chasam Sofer, that every word of Torah and tefillah is a heavenly chamber, and davening ascends through the worlds. Foreign thoughts during davening mean the keruvim are pushing a person out, so before davening one does teshuvah and includes oneself with the tzaddikim and all Jews; davening, especially Shacharis, is a war, with tallis and tefillin as its weapons.

title.en: The beinoni during and after davening

summary.en: The Rav explains that the beinoni is always armed for the war, so during Shema and tefillah the other king has no permission to enter; the Tanya describes this as the time of greatness of mind, contemplating Hashem's greatness in the blessings before Shema. After davening the evil reawakens, but since it is only one of two judges and the good also sits, it cannot bring its desire into action.

title.en: Passer-by, guest, master; the mind rules the heart

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the yetzer has three names, a passer-by, a guest and a master of the house, and says that in the beinoni it always remains a passer-by who is turned away at the door. The reason, from the Ra'aya Mehemna, is that the mind by nature rules over the heart, so no one can say his yetzer overpowered him.

title.en: Rare cases where one cannot help himself

summary.en: The Rav adds, noting that this is not in the Tanya, that occasionally Hashem places a person in a situation where he truly cannot control himself and is not responsible; but this is rare, and a person must always suspect that he can help himself. In general the mind rules the heart, and the beinoni says no to every suggestion and pushes the thought away.

title.en: Light drives away darkness

summary.en: The Rav explains that a bad thought is driven away more easily by thinking of holy matters, bringing the passuk in Koheles about the advantage of wisdom over folly like light over darkness. Darkness, he says, is a real creation, as the passuk in Yeshayahu says, yet a little light pushes away much darkness; so the folly of the kelipah is pushed away by the holy thought, and even so the beinoni is not called a tzaddik.

title.en: The yetzer still present; three daily failings

summary.en: The Rav explains that the yetzer still sits on its bench, and after davening the love of Hashem is only hidden, so the yetzer can make suggestions, even of forbidden things, which the beinoni rejects. He brings the Gemara that no one escapes hirhur aveirah and iyun tefillah daily, with Tosafos' reading of iyun tefillah as feeling one has davened well, and concludes that the impression of davening and the hidden love keep the yetzer from ruling.

catalogTitle: בינוני - זה וזה שופטן וה' מכריע. תשובה על הקושיא על המילים - תהא בעיניך כרשע.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the beinoni is judged by two 'judges', the good and evil inclinations, with Hashem as the deciding voice, and how this answers why even a tzaddik should regard himself as a rasha.

abstract.en: Finishing Tanya chapter 12, the Rav explains that the beinoni cannot stop thoughts of envy, hatred or resentment from arising, but has the choice not to accept them. Emunah that everything comes from Hashem removes resentment, as David said of Shimi ben Gera and as Yosef repaid his brothers with good; a tzaddik told a shopkeeper to thank Hashem for every customer who went to his competitor. Moving to chapter 13, he explains the Gemara's 'zeh v'zeh shoftan': the yetzer hara is a judge giving an opinion, not a ruler, and Hashem is the decider who helps the good side. The world is balanced between good and evil, but the Creator stands above it, as light drives out darkness. Hashem helps only one who struggles himself. This answers 'be in your eyes like a rasha': without Hashem's help the yetzer would win. Finally, the beinoni's evil is only asleep during prayer, which explains Rabbah's error in calling himself a beinoni.

en: The beinoni cannot prevent bad thoughts from arising, but he has the choice not to accept them willingly and to push them out at once.
Resentment toward someone who caused harm contradicts emunah, since everything that happens to a person is decreed from Heaven and the other person is only the stick.
The yetzer hara in the beinoni is a judge who states his opinion, not a ruler who must be obeyed, and the halachah follows the decider, Hashem, who helps the yetzer tov.
Hashem's help comes only to one who struggles against the yetzer hara himself, like the mitzvah to help unload an animal only together with its owner.
'Be in your eyes like a rasha' means that even one who does no sin should know that the yetzer in him is as strong as in a rasha, and only Hashem's help keeps him from falling.
During Krias Shema and tefillah the beinoni's evil is only asleep, subdued but not transformed, and it can wake up again afterwards.

title.en: The beinoni's choice over passing thoughts

summary.en: The Rav explains from Tanya chapter 12 that thoughts of envy, hatred and resentment come to the beinoni on their own, but he can refuse to accept them and push them away. He adds that resentment toward another Jew goes against emunah, since whatever happens is decreed from Heaven.

title.en: Shimi, Yosef and the competing shop

summary.en: The Rav brings David HaMelech's response to Shimi ben Gera, the mashal of the dog that bites the stick, and Yosef repaying his brothers with good. He then tells of a tzaddik who told a man to thank Hashem each time a customer entered his competitor's shop, until the thanks became true in his heart.

title.en: Two judges and the One who decides

summary.en: Starting chapter 13, the Rav explains the Gemara's 'zeh v'zeh shoftan' from the plural 'shoftei nafsho': the yetzer hara is like a judge voicing an opinion from the heart, not a ruler, and the yetzer tov argues against it. The halachah follows the decider, Hashem, as the Gemara says that without His help one could not overcome the yetzer.

title.en: A balanced world and the light that drives out darkness

summary.en: The Rav brings a teaching of the Maggid Meisharim that Hashem is the decider who helps the tzaddik, who still receives full credit at the judgment. He explains that the world's good and evil are balanced, as the Gemara shows from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya, but the Creator stands above the balance, just as light does not mix with darkness but drives it out.

title.en: Then how can anyone sin?

summary.en: The Rav asks: if Hashem always sides with the good, how can a person ever sin? He answers from the mitzvah of 'azov ta'azov imo', which applies only when the owner works along: Hashem helps only one who struggles against the yetzer hara himself, and so the beinoni who fights never sins.

title.en: Answering 'be in your eyes like a rasha'

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem's help is the light of Hashem in the G-dly soul, which pushes away the darkness, as Yosef was helped when he could no longer resist. With this he answers the question from Tanya's first chapter: the tzaddik should see himself like a rasha because the yetzer in him is just as strong, and only Hashem's help keeps him from sinning.

title.en: The yetzer hara is not gone, only quiet

summary.en: The Rav explains that the beinoni's evil keeps its full strength, and every physical act strengthens it further. Only during Krias Shema and tefillah, or for one who learns Torah lishmah all day, does the yetzer have no voice, yet even then it is not driven out but only asleep.

title.en: Subdued, not transformed: Rabbah's error

summary.en: The Rav explains that even in prayer the G-dly soul only rules over the animal soul like a wrestler on top, which is iskafya rather than transformation; only a tzaddik like David HaMelech, whose heart was 'chalal', has killed the evil. This answers Tanya's question of how Rabbah could call himself a beinoni: his whole day of learning was like the time of Krias Shema.

catalogTitle: כח התורה: Torah Missiles

oneLiner.en: With a war looming at the start of Adar, the Rav teaches through the Chasam Sofer that when troubles contradict each other the only protection is Torah, and that the Jewish people's real weapons are Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens on Rosh Chodesh Adar with a war about to break out, noting that Adar is a month of strong mazal for Jews and that they too must gather forces: malachim created by Torah, mitzvos and tefillah. He tells from the Chasam Sofer's diary, Sefer Hazikaron, how Napoleon's siege of Pressburg killed hundreds of gentiles but only one Jew, an informer, and compares the first Gulf War. He brings the Chasam Sofer's reading of the passuk about many troubles: the Gemara allows praying for only one trouble at a time, but when troubles contradict like a bee sting and a scorpion sting, one cannot pray for peace since war may begin the geulah. The answer is the 'shira', the Torah, which protects. Tehillim 149 shows that the Jews' war is fought with the mouth. Finally he explains why Achashverosh, and in his view Bush, came to power against the people's will: Hashem appointed them for His purpose.

en: Adar is a month of strong mazal for Jews, and just as an army gathers soldiers, Jews must gather forces of malachim created by Torah, mitzvos and tefillah.
In the Chasam Sofer's time, Napoleon's bombardment of Pressburg killed hundreds of gentiles but only one Jew, who had informed on the Chasam Sofer.
When two troubles contradict each other, like a bee sting and a scorpion sting, one cannot pray for either remedy; this is why one could not simply pray for peace in a war that may bring the geulah.
The Chasam Sofer's answer is 'the shira', meaning the Torah: learning Torah is the protection that works whatever the troubles.
The war's outcome is decided not by presidents and generals but by Jews learning, davening and saying Tehillim, whose weapon is the mouth.
Achashverosh became king by himself and not by election, to make clear that Hashem had appointed him for the miracle of Purim.

title.en: A looming war and the mazal of Adar

summary.en: The Rav opens on Rosh Chodesh Adar with a war about to begin that no leader can predict. He brings the Gemara that a Jew in a dispute with a gentile should seek it in Adar, whose mazal is strong, and says that just as the American army gathers soldiers, Jews must gather malachim through Torah, mitzvos and tefillah.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer's diary of Napoleon's siege

summary.en: The Rav describes the Chasam Sofer's Sefer Hazikaron, a diary of Napoleon's months-long siege of Pressburg: the signs he received beforehand, the yeshiva's learning and daily long Tachanun, and the wonder that only one Jew, an informer, was killed. He compares the first Gulf War, where in Israel the only victim of the Scuds was a man who had been cursed.

title.en: Praying for only one trouble at a time

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk of 'many evils and troubles' that the Chasam Sofer explains, and the Gemara that one may fast and pray for only one trouble at a time. When a city had both plague and hunger, they were told to pray for plenty, since food is given to the living, and so the plague stopped too.

title.en: The bee and the scorpion: contradicting troubles

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara's bee and scorpion: one venom heats and one cools, so a person stung by both cannot be healed, and such troubles will come before Moshiach. The Chasam Sofer applies this to the war: one cannot pray for peace, because war may be the beginning of the geulah, yet the people are suffering.

title.en: Torah is the protection; the war of the mouth

summary.en: The Chasam Sofer answers that 'the shira', the Torah, protects, and the Rav adds tefillah and tzedakah as the Jews' ammunition: the war is decided not by Bush or Saddam but by Jews in batei medrash. He brings Tehillim 149 and the Chazal about Chizkiyahu sleeping calmly on Pesach night while a malach destroyed Sancheirev's camp, showing that the Jews' sword is in their mouth.

title.en: Why Achashverosh made himself king

summary.en: Noting that Bush is pressing for war against the world's opposition, the Rav asks why the Megillah tells that Achashverosh became king by himself, and answers that Hashem appointed him for the salvation of Purim. He compares the Maharal's answer on why the Jews were forced to accept the Torah although they wanted it: what the world depends on is not left to people.

title.en: Involuntary muscles, Bush, and the soldiers of Adar

summary.en: The Rav illustrates the Maharal with the heart and lungs, which work without a person's will because life depends on them, and applies the idea to Bush, who became president with fewer votes, so Hashem made him president for a role. He closes that Adar is a month of war against Amalek, fought with Torah, tefillah, tzedakah and resisting the yetzer hara, and that the listeners are the soldiers who will bring victory to Klal Yisrael.

catalogTitle: יש כמה מדריגות במדריגת אמת. הדרכה וי"ד שלא להיות עצוב כשבאים אצלו מחשבות רעות ועצה איך להתחזק כנגדם.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that truth has many levels, so the beinoni's prayer is true by his own measure, and that a beinoni should not be saddened by bad thoughts but fight them through the hidden love every Jew has for Hashem.

abstract.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 13, the Rav explains why a beinoni's love in prayer is not called 'avodas emes' compared to tzaddikim: truth is lasting, as 'sfas emes tikon la'ad', and a fervor that gives way to desire after davening shows it lacked truth. Yet truth has levels. Yaakov, the attribute of truth, is the middle bar running through all the boards of the Mishkan, each board a level of Jews, so what is falsehood for a higher person is truth for a lower one. He brings the Yismach Moshe's answer to the Rema: every Jew has his own reading of the Torah by his level. Moving to chapter 14, he teaches that a beinoni must not feel bad about bad thoughts; he should rejoice at the chance to fulfil 'lo sasuru', strengthen himself with the hidden love that makes even simple Jews give their lives, and fight every sin.

en: Truth is what endures: a tzaddik's fervor in prayer that gives way to desire for this world afterward shows that it lacked truth.
Truth has levels: what would be falsehood for a higher person is true service for a lower one, according to his level.
Every Jew has his own reading of the Torah according to his level, as the Yismach Moshe answers the question on the Rema.
A beinoni should not feel bad when bad thoughts come to him even after good preparation for davening; this is how he was created and his mission in the world.
When a bad thought comes he should rejoice, since pushing it away fulfils the mitzvah of 'lo sasuru' and breaks the sitra achra.
Every Jew, even the worst, has a hidden love for Hashem that would make him give his life rather than serve idols; he sins only because a spirit of folly makes him forget it.

title.en: Why the beinoni's prayer is not called truth

summary.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 13, the Rav explains that the beinoni subdues evil only during prayer, and that relative to tzaddikim this is not 'avodas emes'. Truth, he explains from 'sfas emes tikon la'ad', is lasting, while falsehood and the pleasures of this world are momentary and leave a person empty.

title.en: Yaakov, the middle bar of the Mishkan

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov, the attribute of tiferes, is the middle bar that runs from end to end through the boards of the Mishkan, each board being a level among Jews. He reads the names Yisrael and Yaakov as spanning head to heel, and brings the Yerushalmi that the boards had a fixed order, marked by writing, which may not be changed.

title.en: Each level has its own truth

summary.en: Since Yaakov's attribute of truth passes through every board, the Rav concludes that each Jew has his own level of truth. For a tzaddik, desire returning after prayer shows the prayer was falsehood; for a beinoni, being cleaved to Hashem during prayer alone is the truth of his level, as the Tanya says.

title.en: Every Jew's own reading of the Torah

summary.en: From 'darosh darash', the middle of the Torah in the week's parsha, the Rav learns that every Jew has his own interpretation of the Torah by his level. He illustrates it with the Rema that one who is 'mafleg bachasidus' may give his life even for other mitzvos, and the Yismach Moshe's answer to how this fits 'vachai bahem'.

title.en: Two readings of 'sfas emes tikon la'ad'

summary.en: The Rav applies this to the passuk 'sfas emes tikon la'ad': for the great tzaddik it means truth that never fades, while for the beinoni it means truth that is stored away until his next prayer. He reads the Tanya's words that the attribute of truth is Yaakov's, the middle bar and a 'heritage without bounds', reaching every level, and illustrates with how a twelve-hour learning day is judged differently for the Chofetz Chaim and for a young bochur.

title.en: Chapter 14: the beinoni and free choice

summary.en: Having finished the Tanya's foundations, the Rav begins chapter 14: the beinoni never acts on the yetzer hara's words though he hears them, and he should not feel bad that bad thoughts come after davening, since this is how he was created. Being repulsed by evil is not always in a person's power, but his thought, speech and action always are.

title.en: Rejoicing at the mitzvah of 'lo sasuru'

summary.en: The Rav teaches that the first bad thought is not in a person's control and he need not feel bad about it; on the contrary, he should rejoice, since pushing it out fulfils 'lo sasuru acharei levavchem', one of the greatest mitzvos, which breaks the sitra achra. He then reads the Tanya's declaration that one does not want to be separated from Hashem but to cleave to Him with thought, speech and action.

title.en: The hidden love and the spirit of folly

summary.en: The Rav explains the hidden love, mentioned here for the first time in the Tanya: every Jew, even a wicked one, has it, and at a time of decree to serve idols simple Jews gave their lives. He asks why such a Jew commits other sins, and answers with the Tanya that a spirit of folly makes him think other sins do not cut him off, so the beinoni resolves to fight the yetzer hara over every sin.

title.en: Love with delight, and the beinoni's work

summary.en: The Rav explains that truly despising evil comes only from 'ahavah betaanugim', which the tzaddik has constantly and the beinoni only at moments, especially on Shabbos and Yom Tov, a gift like 'avodas matanah'. When it is absent, desire for this world fills the void; this answers the question of Iyov 'You created tzaddikim', and the beinoni's work is never to obey the yetzer hara.

catalogTitle: חילוקים בבינונים - עובד ה' ואשר לא עבדו.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's distinction between the beinoni who serves Hashem by constant battle and the beinoni who 'does not serve Him' because his learning comes easily, and shows that real avodah means going beyond one's nature and habit.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by stressing that every beinoni is sent a battle suited to his nature, health, family and surroundings, as Avraham Avinu, born to Terach, had to fight against everything he came from. He then reads the Tanya on the passuk in Malachi that distinguishes between tzaddik and rasha, and between one who serves G-d and one who does not. 'Oved' is present tense: the beinoni is in an ongoing war, while the tzaddik bears the name as a title. The one who 'does not serve' is also a beinoni and never sins, yet wages no war, because he is a masmid by nature or because hidden love inherited from the Avos suffices for him. A masmid by habit was an oved while he worked, but becomes one who does not serve once it is easy. Using the Gemara's 100 versus 101 reviews and the donkey-drivers' mashal, the Rav defines avodah as going beyond habit, through contemplating Hashem's greatness or awakening the hidden love.

en: Each person is given his own battle according to his nature and circumstances, and he should not envy another's soul.
The beinoni is called 'oved Elokim' because he is constantly at war with his yetzer hara, while the tzaddik carries the name as a title.
The one who 'does not serve' is not a rasha; he is a beinoni who never sins, even through bittul Torah, but has no battle to fight.
Whether a person is a masmid by nature or became one through habit, as long as he only does what comes easily he is called 'lo avado'.
Avodah means doing more than one's habit, as the Gemara contrasts reviewing a chapter 100 times with 101 times.
There are two ways to break one's nature: contemplating the greatness of Hashem, or awakening the hidden love in the heart.

He brings Avraham Avinu, born to Terach, who had to fight everything he came from, and says one should not envy another's soul.

title.en: Tzaddik and oved Elokim

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya on the passuk in Malachi and asks how 'tzaddik' and 'oved Elokim' differ. 'Oved' is present tense: the beinoni is still fighting, and with the mashal of a swimmer he shows that toil can feel like pleasure; for the tzaddik, 'oved' is a settled title, since he has already driven out his yetzer hara.

title.en: The beinoni who 'does not serve'

summary.en: The Rav explains that the beinoni has two levels, and the one 'who does not serve' is not a rasha, since he never sins, not even bittul Torah. He is called so because he wages no war: learning and davening come easily to him, perhaps because he was born and raised in holiness, while one who struggles with every sugya earns far more reward.

title.en: The natural masmid and hidden love

summary.en: The Rav explains why the 'lo avado' needs no battle: he is a masmid by nature, with a calm temperament that does not crave the world's excitements, so he need not contemplate Hashem's greatness to overcome his yetzer hara. The hidden love that every Jew has suffices for him, but he makes no effort to become better than he is.

title.en: Avraham Avinu, a new creation

summary.en: The Rav explains that the hidden love is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, whose toil on himself made him a new creation. He brings 'behibaram' read as 'be-Avraham' and the verses said daily in davening, and explains that Avraham is the source of every Jew's love of Hashem and Yitzchak of his fear.

title.en: The masmid by habit; 100 and 101

summary.en: The Rav explains that one who trained himself to be a masmid, with fines and other means, was an oved Hashem while he struggled, but once it became second nature he is 'lo avado'. Such a person can become an oved by learning more than his habit, with more depth, as the Gemara contrasts reviewing 100 times with 101.

title.en: The donkey drivers and the limit

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara's mashal of the donkey drivers, who charge double for going past their regular limit, compares it to taxi fares, and concludes that the hardest thing is to act against one's habit. He cites Rabbi Yisrael that a masmid is one who holds on past the point where it is hard, and explains that forgetting comes from the sitra achra, whose name Samech-Mem equals 100.

title.en: Going beyond habit: two ways

summary.en: The Rav explains that a masmid by nature keeps his fixed schedule but will not learn a minute past mealtime; the oved does more than his habit. Reviewing a 101st time brings one into the realm of Michael, whose name equals 101, and the Rav concludes that nature is broken either by contemplating Hashem's greatness or by fanning the hidden love inherited from Avraham Avinu.

catalogTitle: הבינוני יכול להיות כצדיק בעיתות רצון' עיבור נשמת צדיק בתוכו' כשעושה עצמו שמח בטוב ומואס ברע זוכה שזה נעשה טבעו.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains how a beinoni, who cannot choose to be a true tzaddik, can still fulfill the oath 'be a tzaddik': through moments of real joy in Hashem, through habit that becomes second nature, and through the soul of a tzaddik that comes into him (ibbur).

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the Tanya's distinction: a beinoni wages a constant war with the yetzer hara and every Jew can reach that, but being a tzaddik needs a special soul. This explains the double oath, 'be a tzaddik and do not be a rasha': not being a rasha is in everyone's hands, while 'be a tzaddik' means to strive for it. Still, the Tanya says, a person should set times to contemplate that worldly pleasures are worthless and to rejoice in Hashem; even if passing, at his level it counts. Habit also becomes second nature, as with a brachah said with thought. With the parable of Dovid's harp and a tuned piano string he shows that joy below arouses joy above. Perhaps a spark of a tzaddik's soul will come into him, as in the story of Rav Chaim Vital. A Jew's small mitzvah is multiplied above, which he illustrates with Haman and the omer.

en: Being a beinoni, who never sins though the yetzer hara still fights him, is within every Jew's choice; being a tzaddik is not, since it needs a special soul.
This explains why the oath is doubled: 'do not be a rasha' is an absolute obligation, while 'be a tzaddik' means to strive toward it.
Moments of joy in Hashem that a beinoni reaches through contemplation are not absolute truth, yet relative to his level he fulfills 'be a tzaddik' through them.
Habit rules a person and becomes second nature, so repeated contemplation can make loathing evil and rejoicing in Hashem his nature.
A Jew's joy in serving Hashem below arouses a matching joy above, like two strings tuned to the same note.
Through his own effort the beinoni may merit that the soul of a tzaddik enters him (ibbur), and with its help he serves Hashem with true joy.
A Jew's small mitzvah is multiplied as it rises through the worlds, unlike the deeds of a non-Jew, which stay below.

title.en: Why the oath is doubled

summary.en: The Rav reviews the difference between a tzaddik, who needs a special soul, and a beinoni, whose constant war with the yetzer hara is in every Jew's hands. He uses it to explain the double oath 'be a tzaddik and do not be a rasha', and notes that a Jew can taste joy in Hashem on Shabbos, Yom Tov or during learning, though it does not last.

title.en: Contemplation and habit as second nature

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's 'nevertheless': a person should set times to contemplate that worldly pleasures are worthless and to rejoice in Hashem. Even if this is not absolute truth for a beinoni, at his level he fulfills 'be a tzaddik'; and since habit becomes second nature, the feeling can become truly his.

title.en: A brachah and learning said with thought

summary.en: The Rav gives examples of building the habit: pausing a few seconds before a brachah to think for Whom and why one makes it, and before learning to think that Torah is the wisdom of Hashem. Done regularly, this becomes nature, and an awakening below brings an awakening above.

title.en: Dovid's harp and the tuned string

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that a harp hung over Dovid's bed and played at midnight, and explains it with a piano tuner's fork: a string tuned to the same note vibrates by itself. Dovid was tuned to Gan Eden; likewise a Jew who rejoices in Hashem arouses Hashem's joy in him, as in 'yismach Yisrael' and 'yismach Hashem'.

title.en: Gilgul, ibbur and Rav Chaim Vital's story

summary.en: The Rav explains that a soul which failed through negligence to fulfill mitzvos returns in a full gilgul, while one that missed a mitzvah not by its fault, or a lofty soul that longs for mitzvos, comes into a living Jew for a while as an ibbur and helps him do the mitzvah. He describes unexplained times of great love and closeness as such an ibbur, and tells how Rav Chaim Vital sat on the grave of Benayahu ben Yehoyada and the Arizal stood up for him.

title.en: A tzaddik's soul enters him; the sundial

summary.en: The Rav returns to the Tanya: one who accustoms himself to rejoice in Hashem will play the music of joy on his soul, and perhaps a spirit from above, a spark of a tzaddik's soul, will come into him so that he serves with true joy. This is a third way to fulfill 'be a tzaddik', and the joy he causes above is far greater than what he feels, like a sundial's shadow moving an inch while the sun moves millions of miles.

title.en: Haman's ten thousand talents and the omer

summary.en: The Rav repeats a thought he said at the Pesach seudah: the Gemara tells that Haman found Mordechai teaching the laws of the omer's handful and said it outweighed his ten thousand talents. He explains that a Jew's mitzvah rises and is multiplied through the worlds while a non-Jew's deed stays below, and he distinguishes 'aseres' (a collective, a multiplication) from 'isaron' (a division, as in 'ishon', a small person in the eye).

title.en: The barley omer is lifted up

summary.en: The Rav explains that the omer, brought of barley, animal food, like the minchas sotah, is the cheapest offering, yet it is called the omer of waving because it is lifted up and turns from animal into man, raising the Jews day by day until Shavuos. He concludes that the beinoni's small joy below arouses great joy above, and with the help of the soul that comes into him he fulfills 'be a tzaddik' in truth.

catalogTitle: הספד: על האדמו”ר מסאטמאר זצ”ל

oneLiner.en: In a hesped for the Satmar Rebbe, the Rav describes his tireless avodas Hashem and explains that his fierce battle was for the pure geulah of Moshiach as the Rambam defines it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that although the sun and the earth are unchanged, the world is different after the passing of the Satmar Rebbe, whose voice of Torah and tefillah has been silenced. As a neighbor he would look into the Rebbe's lit windows late at night and before dawn and see him immersed in avodas Hashem; except for Shabbos he never went to bed. He recalls that Rav Reuven Grozovsky consulted him and said the whole Torah was open to him, and that crowds waited for hours for his brachah. Turning to the huge funeral, he explains that the Rebbe was controversial because he feared that Jews would mistake the founding of the state for the geulah. He fought like a lion for the true geulah described by the Rambam, and even an opponent admitted that the Rebbe kept them in check.

en: After the Satmar Rebbe's passing the world is a different world, because the voice of a tzaddik's Torah and tefillah has been silenced.
The Rav saw from his windows that the Rebbe was immersed in avodas Hashem at all hours and, except on Shabbos, never went to bed.
The Rebbe opposed the state because he feared people would mistake its founding for the geulah and treat its leader as Moshiach.
The geulah he awaited was the pure one the Rambam describes, led by a king from the house of David who brings the whole world to serve Hashem together.
Because of his constant fight, Jews still hold on to the belief in the coming of Moshiach as one of the principles of faith.

He lays out the Rambam's description of Moshiach as the geulah the Rebbe awaited, cites an opponent's admission that the Rebbe kept them in check, and concludes that thanks to him Jews still believe in Moshiach.

catalogTitle: עבודת הבינוני - לידע שנברא לעבודת ה'' ושלא לעשות רע. כל יהודי לפי שורש נשמתו.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 16 the Rav explains that a beinoni who cannot feel love of Hashem must at least know it with his mind, and, by way of the dispute between Chabad and the Polish tzaddikim, that every Jew serves Hashem according to the root of his soul, like a letter in its exact place in the Sefer Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens Tanya chapter 16: the beinoni cannot rule his heart, so he must at least know with his mind that he was created to serve Hashem. A tzaddik feels love of Hashem; the beinoni is given a taste only at times of favor, such as Shabbos and Yom Tov. Since love and fear are the wings of every mitzvah, the Rav asks how the beinoni can serve with them, and brings the advice that outward motions awaken inner feeling. This leads to the dispute between Chabad, who served with the mind, and the Polish tzaddikim, who sought hislahavus. Both are right, since each Jew follows his soul's root. The Rav develops this through the counting of Bamidbar: every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah with an exact place, which explains why the son of the Israelite woman was refused a place in Dan's camp. He returns to chapter 16: understanding with the mind that one should love Hashem already counts.

en: The beinoni cannot control his heart, but he can and must know with his mind that he was created to serve Hashem.
Love and fear are the two wings that carry every mitzvah upward, and outward motions such as raising the voice can awaken the inner feeling.
Both Chabad's service with the mind and the Polish tzaddikim's hislahavus are true, because each Jew is drawn to the path of his soul's root.
Every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah, which is why Jews were counted by name and arranged by banner, tribe and family in their exact place.
Before Shavuos each Jew must see that his own letter in the Sefer Torah is kosher and beautiful.
If contemplation does not kindle love in the heart, understanding with the mind that one ought to love Hashem already counts in Heaven.
