title.en: The beinoni must know with his mind

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of Tanya chapter 16: the beinoni cannot rule his heart, so he must at least know with his mind that he was created to serve Hashem. A tzaddik feels love of Hashem, while the beinoni gets a taste only at times of favor, on Shabbos and Yom Tov, as King David asked to visit Hashem's palace.

title.en: Outward motions awaken the heart

summary.en: The Rav explains that love and fear are the two wings of every mitzvah and asks how a beinoni can serve with them. He brings the Mesilas Yesharim's advice that outward motions arouse inner feeling, illustrating with the raised voice of an excited person and with what psychologists say, and warns against strange motions.

title.en: Chabad and the Polish tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav describes the dispute between the Chabad tzaddikim, who served with a cool mind, and the Polish tzaddikim, who sought hislahavus. He recalls an old Lubavitcher chassid who davened word by word with tears in the Stoliner shul in Williamsburg, mentions the Mitteler Rebbe's Kuntres HaHispa'alus, and asks who is right.

title.en: Each soul to its rebbe; Jews as letters

summary.en: The Rav answers that both are the words of the living G-d, each by its root. Hashem matches every talmid to the rebbe of his soul's root, as the heavenly voice decrees matches, and as souls stood together at Sinai. Every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah, and a single missing letter invalidates it.

title.en: Counted by names, not numbers

summary.en: The Rav explains why Jews are counted in parshas Bamidbar before Shavuos: each Jew is a letter of the Torah, as the early sages were called soferim for counting its letters. They were counted 'by names', not numbers, like children who are called by name while cattle are branded with numbers, so that each Jew is set in his exact place.

title.en: The camps as the five books

summary.en: The Rav explains the arrangement of the banners: the camps correspond to the five books of the Torah, with the Kohanim and Leviim in the middle corresponding to Vayikra. The Leviim numbered twenty-two thousand, matching the twenty-two letters of the alef-beis, and every Jew stood by his banner as his soul is placed in the Torah.

title.en: The son of the Israelite woman

summary.en: The Rav asks why the son of the Israelite woman was refused a place in Dan's camp when the desert was large, and answers that he was not a letter of the Sefer Torah. Even a ger can be a crown on the letters, as Rabbi Akiva, from a family of gerim, expounded the crowns, but according to the Gemara's other account this man mocked the lechem hapanim and was an apikores, so he had no connection at all.

title.en: Each Jew in his place before Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav concludes that before Shavuos each Jew must make his letter in the Sefer Torah kosher and beautiful, and returns to the dispute: every Jew belongs to his place, and Hashem arranges that each is drawn to Chabad, to Belz or to Rav Shach according to the family of letters his soul belongs to. Nothing is by chance.

title.en: Love of Hashem in the mind suffices

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Ba'al haTanya taught that the main thing is the mind, while others stressed the middos, and all are right. He reads Tanya chapter 16: one should contemplate Hashem's greatness in creation, which may kindle love and fear, and if it does not, understanding with the mind that it ought to be so is enough and is counted in Heaven as real love.

catalogTitle: תשובה על “כי קרוב אליך הדבר מאד” - איך אהבת ה' ויראת ה' קרוב לבינוני. די להם אהבה ויראה שכליות' בלי הרגשים גדולים שיש לצדיקים.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, on Tanya chapter 16, how serving Hashem stays 'very near' even for a beinoni who cannot feel love and fear in his heart: love and fear understood in the mind become the wings that lift his Torah and mitzvos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the title page of the Tanya, which is built on the verse 'ki karov eilecha hadavar meod', and recalls the earlier chapters: contemplating Hashem's greatness with chochmah and binah gives birth to love and fear, which comes easily to tzaddikim. For a beinoni whose heart does not catch fire, the Tanya in chapter 16 gives a great rule: love and fear that he understands with his mind are also enough. Along the way he speaks about true stories of tzaddikim, tells the Yismach Moshe's dream of tasting the Rambam's yiras shamayim, and describes the overwhelming fear of Reb Zusha, Reb Shlomo of Karlin and Reb Shmelke. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on why Hashem held the mountain over Klal Yisrael at Sinai, explains why Chazal say a good thought is 'joined' to the deed, and ends with the simple Jew whose hidden love lifts his mitzvos as far as olam haYetzirah.

en: The whole Tanya is built on the verse that serving Hashem is 'very near', and the Rav shows how this holds for every person according to his level.
A beinoni who cannot bring his love and fear into the feeling of the heart still serves Hashem properly with love and fear understood in the mind.
When this understanding moves him to learn and do mitzvos, it becomes the wings that lift his Torah and mitzvos, as if he had served with felt love and fear.
By nature a thought of the mind cannot join a physical deed and lift it; Hashem joins them, and this is the meaning of 'a good thought Hashem joins to the deed'.
Mitzvos done from felt love and fear rise to olam haBeriah; those done from understanding are joined there by Hashem; those done from habit rise through hidden love only to olam haYetzirah.

candidateTopics: intellectual love and fear of Hashem

title.en: 'Very near' for each according to his level

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Tanya's title verse 'ki karov eilecha hadavar meod' and recalls how contemplation with chochmah and binah gives birth to love and fear, easily for tzaddikim. He asks what the beinoni should do, answers that understood love and fear are enough, and brings the Yismach Moshe that 'vachai bahem' means something different for each person's level. He then begins the text of chapter 16.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe tastes the Rambam's fear

summary.en: The Rav praises true stories of tzaddikim as a way to bring a person close to Hashem, recommends the Tehilla LeMoshe, and tells the Yismach Moshe's dream in which he asked to feel the yiras shamayim of great figures and could not bear even the Rambam's fear from a time of katnus. He explains through the beat of the heart that every person goes through rising and falling.

title.en: The overwhelming feelings of tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav describes the fear of Reb Zusha, the Ba'al HaTanya's words about Reb Shlomo of Karlin's constant fear, and Reb Shmelke, who had to be shaken out of his dveikus. He explains that tzaddikim felt this because their pure souls had no insulation blocking the current.

title.en: When the heart cannot feel

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya on one whose contemplation of Hashem's greatness never reaches the feeling of the heart. His mind still understands that his soul should yearn to Hashem, that the soul stays in the body like a living widow, and that Hashem is grasped only through Torah and mitzvos, like embracing a clothed king.

title.en: Understanding gives the mitzvos wings

summary.en: The Rav explains why the Tanya says understood love and fear are also good: the understanding moves a person to learn and do mitzvos, and it becomes the two wings that lift them, as the Zohar says. A thinking person could busy himself with other wisdom or chess; that his mind leads him to Torah gives his learning the same aliyah.

title.en: Why Hashem held the mountain over them

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's question why Hashem held the mountain over Klal Yisrael at Sinai after they said 'na'aseh v'nishma'. The Torah was given for all generations, including people who must force themselves to learn and serve; forcing oneself is good, and the coercion at Sinai was for them.

title.en: Hashem joins the good thought to the deed

summary.en: The Rav asks why Chazal say 'a good thought Hashem joins to the deed' instead of the usual 'it is as if he did it', and answers that Chazal's words carry a second intention. Felt love comes from the physical heart and can lift the physical deed; a thought of the mind cannot by nature, so Hashem joins it, and the mitzvah rises to olam haBeriah.

title.en: The simple Jew's hidden love

summary.en: The Rav describes a simple Jew who does mitzvos out of habit from his chinuch, without thought. His mitzvos still rise, because they come from the hidden love in every Jew, but only to olam haYetzirah. He closes, partly garbled, with the idea that each mitzvah has many layers, and the inner part meant for olam haBeriah stays below.

catalogTitle: מדריגת יראה ואהבה בדרך 'לעשותו' - יכולים הכל לעשותו' חוץ רשעים עד שיעשו תשובה.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 17, the Rav explains that the Torah's promise that serving Hashem is 'close, in your mouth and your heart, to do it' is kept through a love and fear born in the mind that lead to action, open to every Jew except a rasha until he does teshuvah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the difficulty Tanya chapter 17 resolves: the Torah says the matter is close 'in your heart', yet only tzaddikim rule their hearts. The answer, he explains, lies in the word 'la'asoso', to do it: a love and fear that the mind grasps through contemplating Hashem's greatness and that bring a person to act, even without feeling. He shows how the order of davening is built on this. The mind is in a person's control; only a rasha, whose heart rules him, cannot begin lasting avodah until he does the lower teshuvah, breaking the kelipah with a broken heart and raising the fallen lower hei. This leads to the exile of the Shechinah, the tale of Reb Zusha and the hay, and the Jew's inner exile. He then applies the chapter: when feeling is closed, as with the meraglim and Avraham's tenth trial at the akeidah, one must go with the mind. He ends with Tamuz and Av.

en: The Torah's 'close in your heart, to do it' refers to a love and fear that the mind grasps and that bring a person to keep the mitzvos, even when the heart feels nothing.
A person's mind is in his control even when his heart is not, so contemplating Hashem's greatness is within everyone's reach.
A rasha, whose heart rules him, cannot begin avodah that lasts until he first does the lower teshuvah, breaking the kelipah with a broken heart.
The lower teshuvah raises the fallen lower hei of Hashem's Name, which is the exile of the Shechinah.
When the heart is closed, even in the holiest place or moment, one must serve with the mind; this was Avraham's tenth trial and the trial the meraglim failed.

candidateTopics: intellectual love and fear of Hashem
teshuvah tata'ah and the fallen hei

title.en: How can the heart be 'close'?

summary.en: The Rav raises the difficulty with the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od, beficha uvilvavcha la'asoso': the Gemara calls fear of Heaven a small thing only for Moshe, yet the Torah is eternal, and only tzaddikim rule their hearts. He recalls that the previous chapter began the answer.

title.en: Love and fear in the mind; the order of davening

summary.en: The Rav reviews chapter 16: one who cannot arouse feeling in his heart still achieves enough when his mind understands, through contemplating Hashem's greatness, that one must love and fear Him. He shows how davening follows this path, from korbanos and ketores through the greatness of creation and the angels in birchos krias shema, up to ahavah rabbah and Shema.

title.en: 'La'asoso': the mind rules, except for resha'im

summary.en: Reading chapter 17, the Rav explains that 'la'asoso' means a love that brings to action: the mind is in a person's control, so anyone can contemplate Hashem's greatness and reach an intellectual love that drives the mitzvos. Resha'im are different: they are in the power of their hearts, unlike tzaddikim whose hearts are in their power, so the Torah's words speak of living Jews.

title.en: A rasha needs teshuvah first; the fallen hei

summary.en: The Rav explains that a rasha may do a mitzvah, even a great one, but it flares and goes out; to begin lasting avodah he must first break the kelipah through the lower teshuvah, the 'broken spirit' of the passuk as the Zohar reads it, which raises the fallen lower hei. He tells of Reb Zusha and the peasant's fallen hay, and distinguishes the lower teshuvah from the higher one.

title.en: The Shechinah in exile with the Jew

summary.en: The Rav explains the exile of the Shechinah through Chazal's 'galu le'Edom, Shechinah imahem' and the passuk 'veshav Hashem Elokecha es shevuscha', which says Hashem Himself returns. On the level of remez, a Jew who acts like Edom drags the spark of G-dliness within him into exile in the kelipah; when he does teshuvah with a broken heart the kelipah breaks like a nutshell and the Shechinah rises from her fall.

title.en: When feeling is absent: Eretz Yisrael and the meraglim

summary.en: The Rav ties the chapter back to the previous one: intellectual love and fear, without feeling, is also good, and one cannot always feel. He brings R' Avraham of Kalisk's warning to those traveling to Eretz Yisrael that they may feel nothing and must toil, and the Chasam Sofer's explanation of the meraglim's complaint that they had not felt the land's holiness, which they should have answered with tefillah.

title.en: Avraham's tenth trial and the meraglim

summary.en: The Rav links the meraglim, the tenth trial of the generation of the desert, to Avraham's tenth trial. The akeidah's test was not self-sacrifice, which Avraham had shown long before, but a closed heart: he saw the Place 'from afar', full of questions and assailed by the Satan. The meraglim faced the same test in the land and did not know to break through the shell.

title.en: Serving with the mind when the heart is closed

summary.en: The Rav draws the lesson of the two chapters: when the heart and feelings will not cooperate, one must go with the mind. Even at Ne'ilah or the height of Shabbos the heart may close, and that is Avraham's trial; every honest Jew who is not a rasha can serve this way, and one who finds himself in a rasha's state must break himself through teshuvah.

title.en: Tamuz and Av: the two eyes

summary.en: The Rav connects parshas Shelach to blessing Rosh Chodesh Tamuz: Tamuz and Av, the 'days of the first grapes', are under the dominion of the sitra achra, given to Esav while Yaakov took the other months. They correspond to the two eyes, and are the months for breaking the sitra achra with a broken spirit.

catalogTitle: נשים: Marriage - a Union of קדושה and נצחיות

oneLiner.en: From Parshas Chayei Sarah the Rav shows that a Jewish marriage is a union of kedushah and eternity, and that a Jewish home, its clothing and its toil for chesed are an extension of the Beis HaMikdash.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by explaining why he speaks in English, with the Chazon Ish's parable that the battlefront moves, and the teaching that the Torah was explained in seventy languages. He then asks why a sedra that opens with Sarah's passing is called Chayei Sarah, and why the word for Avraham's weeping has a small kaf. His answer: a Jewish shidduch is decreed before birth, a reunion of souls, and death does not end it. Avraham prepared the Me'aras HaMachpelah as a home where the couple stays united, so Sarah remains alive as his wife. In a personal note he thanks the community for the home they built him, whose soul is the love put into it, like the Beis HaMikdash. Through Tehillim 128 and Rav Hirsch he teaches that every Jewish home is an extension of Tziyon, with a dress code like the Kohanim. He ends with Rivka's chesed and two stories showing that toil for chesed redeems a person from other toil.

en: A Jewish shidduch is decreed before birth; it is a reunion of souls that were already united.
A Jewish marriage is netzach: death separates bodies but not souls, and the couple remains united.
The sedra is called Chayei Sarah because Sarah remains alive as Avraham's wife; her levayah is the introduction to the shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka.
What counts in a building, like the Beis HaMikdash, is its inner soul: the love with which it was built.
Every Jewish home, wherever it is, can be an extension of Tziyon, with its family as Kohanim and its meals bearing the holiness of korbanos.
The clothing and jewelry of a Jewish man and woman, like the Kohanim's garments, must radiate Torah.
Each person is allotted a measure of toil; toil spent on chesed redeems him from other toil.

candidateTopics: the jewish home as an extension of the Beis HaMikdash
tznius and the garments of the Kohanim
teaching in the language children understand

title.en: Why the Rav speaks in English

summary.en: Asked to speak in English, the Rav explains that Yiddish once united Jews but is now spoken only in isolated communities. He tells how the Chazon Ish answered a complaint about a cheder taught in Ivrit with a parable of an old soldier at a battlefront that has moved, and brings the teaching that the Torah was explained in seventy languages: what matters is that it be understood.

title.en: Chayei Sarah: mourning or wedding?

summary.en: The Rav asks why a sedra that opens with Sarah's passing is called Chayei Sarah, and why the kaf of Avraham's weeping is small; he finds the Ba'al HaTurim's answer difficult. Noting that the sedra moves straight from the levayah to the shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka, he asks whether one should mourn or rejoice with it, and answers that the whole sedra is really a wedding, since a shidduch is decreed before birth and is a reunion of souls.

title.en: A marriage that death does not end

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jewish marriage is netzach: the couple is united before birth and after death. Avraham at once prepared the Me'aras HaMachpelah, where each couple lies side by side, as a home where he and Sarah remain united; this explains the small kaf, and why the sedra is called Chayei Sarah. He ties this to kiddushin, to the kesubah's commitment in life and beyond, and calls Sarah's levayah the introduction to the first shidduch in the Torah: kedushah and eternity.

title.en: A personal note: a home with a soul

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk in Shir HaShirim about the apiryon of Shlomo HaMelech and the Alshich's explanation that the gold and silver of the Beis HaMikdash were only its body, while its soul was the flaming love with which it was built. He then thanks the men and boys of Emunas Yisroel, through their wives, for the residence they prepared for him and his wife with so much warmth, and notes that it opens onto the beis medrash.

title.en: Every home an extension of Tziyon

summary.en: Through Tehillim 128 the Rav visits the home of the one who fears Hashem and asks where Tziyon comes in. He reads Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch: such a person sees his home as a branch of the sphere whose center is Yerushalayim. Every home can therefore be an extension of Tziyon, its family Kohanim, and like the Kohanim it has a dress code set by the Torah.

title.en: Rivka's jewelry and her test of chesed

summary.en: The Rav says that the bracelets Eliezer gave Rivka, like her home, had a soul: Torah and the Luchos, which the jewelry radiated. Using what he read about how much water a camel stores, he calculates that watering ten camels meant drawing about four hundred gallons: the demanding test of chesed that showed she was fit for the house of Avraham.

title.en: Toil for chesed redeems other toil

summary.en: Addressing the women of Emunas Yisroel gathered to help kallahs set up their homes, the Rav says such work demands toil, and that each year's toil is decreed on Rosh Hashanah. He tells of Rav Shlomke of Zvhil and the lost gold watch, brings the Gemara that man is born to toil, and tells of a chassid of Rav Aharon of Karlin who suffered in the street what he would not suffer at home. Toil for hachnasas kallah redeems a person from other toil, and he closes with blessings.

catalogTitle: נצחון היצר אינו אלא ע"י שמחה. ביאור “בכל עצב יהיה מותר.” עצות כנגד עצבות.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, on Tanya chapter 26, that the yetzer hara is defeated only through zerizus that comes from simcha, and that sadness over sins belongs only at set times, 'by appointment only'.

abstract.en: The Rav learns Tanya chapter 26. A lazy, heavy fighter loses even to a weaker opponent, as a fierce lion overcomes a stronger ox; so too victory over the yetzer hara comes only through zerizus born of simcha, while atzvus, rooted in the element of earth, takes away the drive to fight. Quoting the Rebbe of Karlin, he says atzvus is no aveirah but leads to aveiros like nothing else. The passuk 'in all sadness there is profit' means only that sadness can lead to joy: regret over sins at set times, 'by appointment only', breaks the ruach hatumah and brings a joy greater than ordinary joy, like light from darkness. He roots simcha in bitachon, explains that suffering comes from the hidden, higher world and must be accepted with joy, and says that sadness during learning, davening or business is a trick of the yetzer hara.

en: Victory over the yetzer hara comes only through zerizus that flows from simcha; atzvus makes a person heavy and lazy.
Atzvus is not itself an aveirah, but nothing brings a person to aveiros as much as atzvus does.
Sadness over one's sins has value only at set times, and only because it leads to the joy that follows it.
Joy that comes after true sadness over sins is greater than other joy, like light that comes out of darkness.
Bitachon is the root of simcha: one who has someone to lean on rejoices, one who is forsaken is sad.
All suffering comes from the hidden world, higher than the revealed one, and is entirely for a person's good, so it is to be accepted with joy.
Sadness over sins that comes during learning, davening or business is a trick of the yetzer hara and must be pushed away.

candidateTopics: simcha and victory over the yetzer hara
regret over sins at set times
bitachon as the source of simcha

title.en: Victory needs zerizus: the lion and the ox

summary.en: The Rav notes that the coming chapters form one subject and begins Tanya chapter 26: in a physical fight, a lazy, heavy fighter is easily beaten even by a weaker opponent. He illustrates with a lion that overcomes a stronger ox or horse through its fierceness and energy, and reads that victory over the yetzer comes only through zerizus that comes from simcha.

title.en: Atzvus: heavy as earth, the way to aveiros

summary.en: The Rav explains that sadness and sluggishness stem from the element of earth, so a sad person lacks the drive to fight the yetzer hara, and brings the Beis Aharon quoting the Rebbe of Karlin that atzvus is no aveirah yet leads to aveiros more than anything. He then explains that 'in all sadness there is profit' does not praise sadness: nothing is created for nothing, and its only profit is the joy that can follow it.

title.en: Regret at set times, then true joy

summary.en: The Rav explains that one who regrets his sins with a bitter heart at set times breaks the ruach hatumah and comes to true joy, comparing it to a businessman who takes inventory of his assets and liabilities. He brings Tehillim 51, Dovid HaMelech's chapter after Nosson HaNavi came to him, which moves from a broken heart to a plea for joy, and the Arizal's custom to say it after Tikkun Chatzos.

title.en: Tikkun Chatzos and light out of darkness

summary.en: The Rav gives the simple reason for the custom, to learn with joy after the sadness of Tikkun Chatzos, describes how Jews once rose at midnight to mourn the Beis HaMikdash, meaning inwardly the mikdash in each Jew's heart, and says today this is not for everyone. He explains that joy after sadness is greater, like light out of darkness, brings the passuk about not serving Hashem with joy, and says that one who did teshuvah may be sure Hashem forgave him, as the bracha 'chanun hamarbeh lisloach' shows.

title.en: Sadness by appointment only

summary.en: The Rav dwells on the Tanya's words 'at set times': like a doctor who sees patients by appointment only, sadness over sins belongs only at fixed times, such as before sleep, erev Shabbos, going to the mikveh, erev Rosh Chodesh or erev Rosh Hashanah, and must otherwise be driven out. He adds that people today are small and this is hard for them, but it is good to know it and take hold of what one can.

title.en: Bitachon, the root of simcha: the two cows

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk 'for in Him our heart rejoices, for in His holy Name we trusted' and tells the story of R' Shimon of Yaroslav and his 'two cows', showing that bitachon is the source of simcha. Following R' Samson Raphael Hirsch's method of related sounds, he links simcha to leaning on someone and atzvus to being forsaken, which is why idols, which give nothing to lean on, are called atzabim.

title.en: Suffering from the hidden world; the port wine

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's advice against sadness over worldly matters, noting that people today are small but can use it at good times. He explains that one blesses for the bad as for the good and accepts it with joy, since it comes from the hidden world, higher than the revealed one, and tells how R' Shalom of Kaminka, after losing a child, asked for port wine, an expensive wine that tastes bitter to one who does not know it.

title.en: All suffering is for one's good

summary.en: The Rav applies the mashal: suffering comes from the hidden world and is entirely for a person's good, because Hashem loves His children and, as the Arizal writes at the start of Etz Chaim, created the world to do good. He brings the passuk 'those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might' and the Gemara that three good gifts are acquired only through suffering, and concludes that even suffering must be accepted with joy.

title.en: Sadness during learning, davening and business

summary.en: The Rav explains that sadness over sins that comes during learning, davening or business must be pushed away, since it is not its time; it is the yetzer hara's trick, because sadness drives a person to taavos, as people unhappy at home console themselves with cake. Thoughts of sin belong at an appointed time, with reflection on Hashem's greatness, after which comes true joy.

catalogTitle: ע"י התבוננות יכולים להגיע ליראה ואהבה מוחית' וזה די למי שאינו יכול להגיע ליראה ואהבה מוחשית. ביאור על תשובה תתאה.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Tanya chapter 18: every Jew, even one who cannot reach love and fear through contemplation, carries a hidden love of Hashem inherited from the Avos, who were the merkavah (chariot) for the Shechinah.

abstract.en: The Rav recalls the previous chapter: contemplating Hashem's greatness, even when it brings only an understanding that one should love and fear Him, is already a level. Tanya chapter 18 adds that even a person of weak mind, who cannot reach this, can serve Hashem with a true heart through the hidden love every Jew inherits from Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov. He compares it to an inherited instinct in animals. The Avos were the merkavah, devoted to Hashem in every act, as were tzaddikim in every generation, illustrated by a story of the Chasam Sofer. He explains Yaakov's years with Lavan as freeing Jewish souls, the counterpart every tzaddik has in kelipah, and the hidden Leah and revealed Rachel. Since we are the Avos' children, even the lowest Jew holds the highest levels hidden, which may surface in his children, and each Jew can become a merkavah through his avodah.

en: Even a person who cannot contemplate Hashem's greatness enough to feel love and fear can keep the mitzvos and learn Torah from the depth of his heart, because of the hidden love in every Jew.
This hidden love is an inheritance from the Avos: love from Avraham, fear from Yitzchak, and the completion of both through Yaakov.
The Avos were the merkavah: they never turned their minds from cleaving to Hashem, and everything they did was devoted to Him; tzaddikim in every generation follow in this.

Since every Jew descends from the Avos, he too has an aspect of merkavah; even the lowest Jew receives at least the nefesh of nefesh of malchus of Asiyah, with chochmah and the light of Ein Sof hidden in it.
Through his avodah a Jew can bring this hidden aspect into the open and make himself, limb by limb, a merkavah for holiness.

candidateTopics: tzaddik and his counterpart in kelipah
Rachel and Leah as revealed and hidden

title.en: Even a weak mind can serve with a true heart

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of Tanya chapter 18 and recalls the previous chapter, that contemplation leading even to an understanding of love and fear is a level. He then explains that even a person who cannot contemplate at all can keep the mitzvos with a true heart, because of the hidden love inherited from the Avos.

title.en: The hidden love as an inherited nature

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew, as a descendant of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, has a hidden love for Hashem even if he does not feel it. He compares it to the instincts animals inherit, like an ox's desire for grass and a lion's for meat, which are part of their very being.

title.en: The Avos are the merkavah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Avos were the merkavah upon which the Shechinah rests, like the Beis HaMikdash in its time, bringing Yechezkel's vision and Yaakov's ladder in the week's parsha. He says tzaddikim in every generation, often hidden, live this way, and tells of the Chasam Sofer, who told his son that even moving a glass on the table was done only according to halachah.

title.en: Yaakov's work with Lavan's sheep

summary.en: The Rav brings the Lechovitcher Rebbe, who would not say Torah on Vayetze because its plain story is itself the greatest Torah. He explains that Yaakov's years with Lavan and his work with the sheep were freeing Jewish souls from the sitra achra, and that Yaakov had to go to the land of the bnei kedem, the place of Bilaam, his counterpart.

title.en: Every tzaddik has a counterpart

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem made a balanced world, so every tzaddik has a counterpart in kelipah: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the gentile sages, Avraham and Nimrod, who was killed the day Avraham died, Yaakov with Esav and Lavan. He then explains the Midrash's 600,000 sheep of Yaakov as the 600,000 Jewish souls, corresponding to the letters of the Torah.

title.en: Yaakov's flock, Leah and Rachel

summary.en: The Rav tells that the Yismach Moshe and the Apter Rav remembered being sheep in Yaakov's flock. He then explains Yaakov's fourteen years of work for Leah and Rachel as two aspects of the Shechinah, the hidden world and the revealed one, and places the hidden love of every Jew in the aspect of Leah.

title.en: Even the lowest Jew draws from the Avos

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya that the Avos are the merkavah and could draw souls to their children from all ten sefiros of the four worlds, and that even the lowest Jew receives at least the nefesh of nefesh of malchus of Asiyah. He explains the levels of nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah and yechidah, the ten sefiros and the four worlds.

title.en: Hidden greatness that surfaces in a child

summary.en: With the example of blond hair that skips a generation, the Rav explains that the greatest levels lie hidden even in the lowest Jew, because the light of Ein Sof is clothed in the chochmah of every Jewish soul. He brings Sefer HaGilgulim that a simple Jew can father a great tzaddik, and explains that Hashem sometimes has a great soul born to an unlikely parent so the Satan will not interfere.

title.en: David's birth; every Jew can be a merkavah

summary.en: The Rav explains that David HaMelech was born in a hidden way so the Satan would not stand in the way, since Moshiach comes from him. He concludes that every Jew, as a grandchild of the Avos, can bring out his hidden powers and make his limbs a merkavah, with the example of guarding the eyes.

catalogTitle: קיץ (for children): Be a Messenger of Hashem on Your Summer Vacation

oneLiner.en: Speaking to boys before summer vacation, the Rav explains that Parshas Shlach is read just as the travel season begins to teach that every trip is a mission from Hashem, to be fulfilled like Yehoshua's successful spies and not like the spies of Moshe.

abstract.en: The Rav contrasts two sets of spies: the meraglim Moshe sent in Parshas Shlach, who failed their mission and brought weeping on Tisha B'Av, and the spies Yehoshua sent to Yericho in the haftarah, who succeeded and are recorded with honor. He notes that the meraglim set out on Erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz, the week after Parshas Shlach, which is exactly when boys say goodbye to their rebbeim and leave for the summer. The Torah's message is that every person who travels is a shliach of Hashem, as the morning bracha 'hameichin mitzadei gaver' says: Hashem prepares every step. Everything in creation has a kind of life and waits for a Jew to come and do a mitzvah with it: a tree for a bracha on its apples or for Torah learned in its shade, water for a bracha, stones that wanted Yaakov to sleep on them, roads to Yerushalayim that mourn. He closes by telling the boys to be good messengers this summer.

en: The meraglim of Parshas Shlach were failed messengers who brought sorrow on Klal Yisrael, while Yehoshua's spies in the haftarah fulfilled their mission and brought success.
The Rav says Parshas Shlach is read just before the summer travel begins because it teaches how to travel: whoever travels is a shliach of Hashem.
The bracha 'hameichin mitzadei gaver' means that Hashem prepares every step a person takes; wherever he goes, Hashem sends him there.
Everything in the world has some life and feeling, and waits for a Jew to come and do a mitzvah with it.
The Rav tells the boys to remember on vacation that they are shluchim: to learn Torah, do mitzvos and behave like a Yid, so Hashem can be proud of them.

title.en: Two sets of spies

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Moshe's meraglim, who left the day before Rosh Chodesh Tammuz, returned on Tisha B'Av and are remembered with dishonor, with the spies Yehoshua sent to Yericho in the haftarah, who succeeded. He notes that the parsha read each week matches the events of that week.

title.en: Every traveler is Hashem's messenger

summary.en: The Rav points out that every year, right after Parshas Shlach, everyone says goodbye to his teachers and goes traveling, just as the meraglim did; this is the parsha's message. He asks the class the meaning of the bracha 'hameichin mitzadei gaver' and explains that Hashem prepares every step, so wherever a person goes he is sent there to do mitzvos.

title.en: All of creation waits for a mitzvah

summary.en: With the image of trees in the mountains waiting for a bracha on their apples or for a boy to learn Torah in their shade, and water waiting for a bracha, the Rav teaches that everything is alive. He brings the stones that wanted Yaakov to sleep on them, the stones of the mizbeach that must not be shamed, and the roads to Yerushalayim that mourn.

title.en: Be a good messenger this summer

summary.en: The Rav applies the lesson to vacation: one goes places not for a suntan or baseball but as Hashem's shliach, to learn, make brachos with kavanah and do chesed. He closes by telling the boys to be successful messengers like Yehoshua's spies, and wishes them a good summer and a return to yeshivah.

catalogTitle: התחלת ביאור אהבה מסותרת. ישתדל להיות מרכבה לה' כפי יכולתו.

oneLiner.en: Opening Tanya chapter 17, the Rav explains how 'the matter is very near to you' holds for every Jew: the mind rules the heart by nature, so service from understanding is always within reach, unless sin has taken away that control, and then teshuvah with a broken heart must come first.

abstract.en: Starting a new zman with chapter 17, the Rav explains that the whole Tanya is built on the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od'. He reviews the earlier chapters: the Jewish soul naturally loves Hashem, as in the mutual love of Shir HaShirim, illustrated by the Avnei Nezer's reason about a bas Levi and by the Lechovitcher, who felt the moment his rebbe passed away. Hisbonenus in the morning brachos should bring forth love and fear, and where it does not burn Hashem counts the cold understanding as the deed. Chapter 17 asks how the Torah can call love of Hashem near when love of Hashem and love of this world cannot live together and only tzaddikim rule their hearts. The answer: the mind rules the heart by nature, so understanding-driven service of mitzvos is near to all, except a rasha who lost control, like Pharaoh. Such a person must first do teshuvah with a broken heart, raising the lower heh of Hashem's Name, which the Rav illustrates with the lulav and esrog and with Yerushalayim and Rome.

en: The whole Tanya is built on the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od, b'ficha uvilvavcha la'asoso', to explain how serving Hashem is near to every Jew.
Because the soul is bound to Hashem, a Jew loves Him by nature and instinct, the mutual love Shlomo HaMelech describes in Shir HaShirim.
Love of Hashem and love of this world's desires cannot live in the heart together; one who is attached to this world only imagines that he loves Hashem.
The mind rules the heart by nature, so a love born of understanding that leads to doing the mitzvos is within reach of every person.
A rasha who sinned until his heart is no longer in his control cannot begin serving Hashem without first doing teshuvah with a broken heart.
Such teshuvah is the lower teshuvah, which raises the last heh of Hashem's Name from its fall and rejoins it to the other three letters.

candidateTopics: natural love of a Jew for Hashem
love of Hashem versus love of this world
loss of free will as punishment
lulav and esrog and the Divine Name

title.en: A new zman: Tanya and 'ki karov'

summary.en: The Rav explains why he starts the new zman at chapter 17, where the part on avodah begins, and asks newcomers to catch up on the earlier groundwork. He shows from the title page that the whole Tanya is built on the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od', explained at length and in brief for each person's level.

title.en: The natural love of a Jew for Hashem

summary.en: Reviewing the earlier chapters, the Rav explains that the soul, a part of G-d above, loves Hashem by instinct, the mutual love of Shir HaShirim, which some say only on Pesach as the Minchas Elazar wrote. He brings the Avnei Nezer's reason why a bas Levi who remarried on false testimony is penalized: the tribe that stayed bound to Hashem at the Egel should have felt that her husband was alive.

title.en: The Lechovitcher feels his rebbe's passing

summary.en: Great tzaddikim felt their bond to Hashem, and even talmidim felt their bond to their rebbe. The Rav tells how the Lechovitcher cried out that he was cut off from his rebbe at the moment Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin was killed, and calmed down once he was told, since a known reason is natural.

title.en: Hisbonenus in the brachos, and the cold intellect

summary.en: The Rav reviews how the mitzvah to love Hashem works: hisbonenus in the brachos of Krias Shema on the angels and on Hashem's love brings forth fear and love, the two wings of every mitzvah, before kabbalas ol malchus Shamayim. Where the flame does not catch, the earlier chapters taught that Hashem counts the cold understanding as if it were felt.

title.en: Chapter 17: is love of Hashem truly near?

summary.en: The Rav opens chapter 17 and asks how the eternal Torah can say love of Hashem is near, when it does not always burn even in great people. Love of Hashem and love of this world cannot share one heart, and he brings the Kotzker's reading of the Targum on 'do not come near a woman' at Matan Torah: one cannot stand on both sides of the fence.

title.en: Only tzaddikim rule their hearts: the answer

summary.en: The Rav strengthens the question from the Gemara that yirah is 'small' only for Moshe Rabbeinu and from Chazal that only tzaddikim have their hearts in their control. The Tanya answers that 'ki karov' means a love of the intellect that brings one to do the mitzvos: everyone with a mind can understand that he must keep the Torah, and this is accepted according to his level.

title.en: The mind rules the heart, unless sin removed it

summary.en: The Rav explains that the mind rules the heart by nature, over the left chamber where the animal soul nests, and can make a person do or refrain from anything if he stops to think. Only a rasha who never used that control loses it as a punishment; the 'reshaim birshus libam'. He brings Pharaoh, whose loss of bechirah at the plagues was the punishment for his earlier sins.

title.en: Teshuvah first: raising the lower heh

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'ki karov' speaks to ordinary people who have not lost their bechirah, while a rasha cannot begin a lasting avodah without teshuvah with a bitter, broken heart that breaks the kelipos. This is teshuvah tata'ah, raising the last heh of Hashem's Name from its exile; he connects it to the four species as the letters of the Name and tells the Rokeach's story of a dream about a separated heh, explained by a man holding the lulav and esrog apart.

title.en: Yerushalayim and Rome, and the separated heh

summary.en: When the soul's sparks are in exile within the kelipah, teshuvah breaks it and separates its forces. The Rav brings Rashi that when one of Yerushalayim and Rome is full the other is ruined, and a remez from a Blazhever tzaddik on Yerushalayim written without a yud in Tanach; as long as the heh is apart the sitra achra is joined, and teshuvah reverses this.

catalogTitle: כל הנשמות הם באים מחכמה שהוא למעלה מהשגה. אמונה מתלבש בחכמה. חידוש המסירת נפש של יהודי על מסירת נפש שיש פעמים אצל הגוים.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, on Tanya chapter 18, that every Jewish soul is rooted in chochmah, the point above understanding where the light of Ein Sof rests, and that this is why even the simplest Jew gives his life rather than deny Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the hidden love that every Jew has, since even the lowest soul is bound to chochmah ila'ah. Reading Tanya chapter 18, he explains that chochmah is not intelligence but the 'koach mah', the first point or flash from which understanding is built, like a drop that grows in the womb into a child. Because the light of Ein Sof rests in chochmah and no thought can grasp Hashem, emunah is above reason, and before Hashem everyone is a 'pesi' who believes. Emunah is a bond of feeling, like a mother's bond to her child, which is why even sinners have given their lives al kiddush Hashem throughout history, as in the story of the Shpoler Zeide's thieves. Non-Jews give their lives through indoctrination; Jews do so without it, from the root. He ends with Parshas Beshalach as the parsha of emunah, Hashem's faithfulness to Klal Yisrael, and Tu Bishvat as the yom tov of emunah.

en: Even the lowest Jewish soul is bound, level above level, to chochmah ila'ah, and therefore carries a hidden love for Hashem.
Chochmah is not intelligence but the source of intellect: the first point or flash, above understanding, from which binah builds a whole structure.
The light of Ein Sof rests in chochmah, and since no thought can grasp Hashem at all, emunah stands above reason and understanding.
Emunah is a bond of feeling and essence, like a parent's bond to a child, and such bonds are stronger than bonds built on understanding.
Therefore even the simplest and most sinful Jews have, throughout history, given their lives rather than deny Hashem.
Non-Jews give their lives through training and indoctrination, while Jews do so without being taught and without understanding, from the root of their soul.
Emunah also means faithfulness: Hashem is faithful to Klal Yisrael, and Parshas Beshalach, read near Tu Bishvat, is the parsha of emunah.

candidateTopics: chochmah as the source of intellect

title.en: Review: the hidden love in every Jew

summary.en: The Rav reviews the previous chapters: every Jew, even the lowest, has a hidden love for Hashem, since his soul is bound level by level up to chochmah ila'ah. Having spoken of those whose love is revealed, the Tanya now turns to those in whom it is completely covered.

title.en: What chochmah really is

summary.en: Reading the Tanya, the Rav explains that chochmah is not intelligence but the source of intellect, the first point above understanding, compared to the father's drop that the mother builds into a child. He illustrates it with the sudden flash of insight into a difficult Tosafos or Rambam, cites the Chovos HaLevavos that chochmah is close to prophecy, and the Arizal's reading of chochmah as 'koach mah'.

title.en: Emunah above understanding

summary.en: Since the light of Ein Sof rests in chochmah and no thought can grasp Hashem, emunah is above reason. The Rav compares trying to grasp Hashem with the mind to trying to see music with stronger eyes, explains 'pesi ya'amin lechol davar' as a quality before Hashem, and brings Dovid HaMelech's words that he was like a beast before Hashem and thereby always with Him.

title.en: A bond of feeling and mesirus nefesh in history

summary.en: The Rav explains that emunah is a bond of feeling, like a mother's bond to her child, stronger than the bond of a teacher and student. Reading the Tanya that even the lowest Jews give their lives al kiddush Hashem, he recounts the generations of shmad: the expulsion from Spain, the refugees taken in by Poland, and whole communities killed in the Crusades with hardly any exception.

title.en: The Shpoler Zeide's thieves

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jew's mesirus nefesh comes from his emunah rooted in chochmah ila'ah, and tells of the thieves among the Shpoler Zeide's followers who were caught, tortured and killed al kiddush Hashem with joy rather than convert.

title.en: Non-Jewish self-sacrifice: training and indoctrination

summary.en: The Rav asks what is special about Jewish mesirus nefesh when non-Jews also give their lives, and answers that soldiers and others are trained and talked into it. He illustrates the old loyalty to a king with a story of a chassid of the Ba'al HaTanya who saw a soldier whipped for frozen ears, and of an old soldier who told the king that the service warms, not the blood.

title.en: Without understanding, from the root; emunah as faithfulness

summary.en: Continuing the Tanya, the Rav explains that sinning Jews who were never taught and do not understand still refuse to deny Hashem, because Hashem's light rests in their chochmah, above reason. He adds that the word emunah means both belief and faithfulness, and that Hashem is faithful to the Jews as they are to Him.

title.en: Parshas Beshalach and Tu Bishvat: the time of emunah

summary.en: The Rav shows that Parshas Beshalach is entirely about emunah, from the splitting of the sea to the war with Amalek, explains 'mah titzak elai' as Klal Yisrael's rescue coming from its root in atika, and mentions the custom of eating kasha. He closes with the Sanzer Rav's words on the yamim tovim from Tu Bishvat to Shavuos, and Tu Bishvat as the yom tov of emunah when the sap rises in the root.

catalogTitle: מסירת נפש של יהודי בא מחמת טבעו. (instinct) כי ה' שורשו.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, through Tanya chapter 19, that even the simplest Jew is ready to give his life for Hashem out of a nature above reason, like a flame that strains upward to its root.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the fact that even the emptiest Jews have given their lives for emunah, unlike gentiles who die for their causes only after being indoctrinated. A Jewish soul comes from chochmah, which is above daas, and there all Jews are equal; that is why Jews said 'na'aseh' without asking reasons. Tanya chapter 19 explains this with 'the candle of Hashem is the soul of man': every thing is drawn to its root, earth falls down and fire rises toward the element of fire. A flame strains upward although reaching its root would end it, because this is its teva, a word for what cannot be explained. So the soul longs to cling to Hashem. The Rav applies this to Adar and Purim, when the lowest Jews show their bond to Hashem. He then explains that holiness comes from chochmah, which means bittul, while kelipah says 'I am something', and illustrates it with the kallah's bittul and with the merchant, the 'Canaani'.

en: Even the simplest and most sinful Jews have given their lives for emunah, which cannot be explained by indoctrination as it is among gentiles.
The Jewish soul is rooted in chochmah, which is above daas; there all Jews are equal, and their bond to Hashem works like an instinct.
Every thing is drawn to its root: earth falls to the ground, while fire strains upward to the element of fire beneath the sphere of the moon.
A flame strains upward although reaching its root would end its separate existence; this is its teva, a word for what has no further explanation.
Likewise the soul longs to part from the body and cling to Hashem, a longing that is above reason and comes from chochmah.
Holiness comes from chochmah and means bittul to Hashem, while kelipah is the feeling of being a separate 'something'.

candidateTopics: soul as the candle of Hashem

title.en: Why simple Jews give their lives

summary.en: The Rav recalls that even the emptiest Jews have died al kiddush Hashem, contrasting this with gentiles who die for falsehood after being indoctrinated. He explains that the Jewish soul is rooted in chochmah, above daas, as shown by 'na'aseh' and by a mother's instinct for her child, and introduces Tanya chapter 19.

title.en: Every thing is drawn to its root

summary.en: Reading 'the candle of Hashem is the soul of man', the Rav explains that all things are drawn to their root: solid things fall because they are mostly earth, like iron drawn to a magnet, while fire rises to the element of fire under the sphere of the moon. He shows from bedikas chametz at night how a flame pulls upward and flickers.

title.en: Fire, Torah and the soul that sways

summary.en: The Rav tells of a gadol who identified a Jewish child exchanged with a gentile one by who would sway over the Gemara, because Torah is fire, and brings the Zohar that a Jew sways because his soul pulls upward. He reads the Tanya on the flame and asks why fire seeks to rise when it would be extinguished, against every creature's instinct of self-preservation.

title.en: The soul's longing is its nature

summary.en: The Rav explains that the flame and the soul, with all its levels, long to reunite with their root although they would lose their existence there. He defines teva as the name for what cannot be explained further, illustrating it with a child asking his mother why things fall, and reads the Tanya that this longing comes from chochmah, above reason.

title.en: Adar, Purim and the lowest Jews

summary.en: Speaking of the coming Purim in Adar Sheni, the Rav explains that Purim was made for the weakest Jews: the months descend from Nissan to Adar, Amalek attacks the stragglers, and in the Purim story the miracle came for the lowest Jews. Purim shows that even the smallest Jew is bound to Hashem above reason, which is why its mitzvah is drinking until 'ad delo yada'.

title.en: Chochmah as bittul, kelipah as 'I am something'

summary.en: Reading the Tanya that all holiness comes from chochmah, which is batel to Hashem, the Rav explains that bittul and lowliness are the essence of a Jew, while kelipah says 'I am something' and is like chametz. He explains chochmah as 'ko'ach mah', the power of nothingness, and brings 'wisdom gives life' to show that chochmah is life.

title.en: Kallah, sitra achra and the merchant

summary.en: The Rav explains that Klal Yisroel is batel to Hashem as a kallah to her chosson, while in the sitra achra the female is stronger, bringing the Or HaChaim on Vayechi. He then explains why a 'Canaani' means a merchant: the chesed of kelipah gives only in order to receive, unlike holy chesed which gives.

catalogTitle: פרקי אבות The Evils of a תלמיד חכם with Bad מדות: צד א: כל הלומד תורה לשמה וכו' נקרא ריע, אהוב, אוהב 'את המקום וכו צד ב: משמח את המקום' משמח את הבריאות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the Mishnah in Avos that one who learns Torah lishmah is a friend and beloved of Hashem and of people, and warns that Torah learning without good middos makes a person worse.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah that one who learns Torah lishmah is called a friend and beloved, loving Hashem and people. Every person longs to love and be loved, and the Torah channels this through two mitzvos: loving one's fellow and loving Hashem. All creatures deserve love because Hashem made them. Love between friends is the precondition for love of Hashem, as a story of two friends and a king shows, and shirah, like the malachim's, needs harmony. Through the Medrash on Shir HaShirim and a mashal of a car dealer he shows how priceless Hashem's love for a tzaddik is. He explains how love can be commanded, how Torah clothes a person in anavah and conditions him to be a tzaddik, with stories of tzaddikim kept from forbidden food. On the second side he stresses that learning without menschlichkeit makes a person worse, bringing the four animals with one kosher sign and the yetzer hara disguised as 'Yesh'.

en: The Rav says every person has a built-in need to love and be loved, and the Torah turns it into avodas Hashem through the mitzvos of loving one's fellow and loving Hashem.
Love of creatures flows from the fact that Hashem created them, since He creates only what He likes; this reaches even a non-Jew, who has a tzelem Elokim, and even animals and insects.
Without love between friends there can be no love of Hashem, and shirah, which means harmony, is possible only among beings who love each other.
Hashem's love for one who learns Torah lishmah is beyond any price, and every Jew has this love in potential, which Torah learning brings out.
Torah lishmah clothes a person in anavah and prepares him to be a tzaddik, and Hashem guards tzaddikim from stumbling even unknowingly.
The Rav stresses that learning without being a mensch makes a person worse, and that a talmid chacham must be seen by people as a decent human being.

title.en: The Mishnah and the human need to love

summary.en: The Rav reads the Mishnah that one who learns Torah lishmah is called a friend and beloved, and explains that tzaddikim use the inborn desire to love and be loved for its true purpose. He explains why one must love all creatures, even a non-Jew and even insects, because Hashem made them.

title.en: Love of friends and the king who joined

summary.en: The Rav says there can be no love of Hashem without love between friends, and tells of two friends in Rome, each ready to die for the other, whom the king asked to take into their friendship. He adds that malachim can sing shirah only because they love each other, since shirah means harmony.

title.en: Malachim, the classroom, and the shirah at the Yam Suf

summary.en: The Rav contrasts competition in a classroom with the malachim who give each other permission to sing out of love. At the splitting of the sea the Yidden sang shirah in place of the malachim, so they too needed that love, which is the key to a connection with Hashem.

title.en: A love no wealth can buy

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk in Shir HaShirim that many waters cannot extinguish the love between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and the Medrash of a tzaddik's coffin that floated in the air. With a mashal of a customer offering a few dollars for an expensive car, he explains why offering all one's wealth for that love would be scorned, and says one reaches it through Torah lishmah.

title.en: Can love be commanded; anavah as a garment

summary.en: The Rav answers the bochurim's question how the Torah can command a feeling: every Jew has the love in potential, and Torah lishmah makes it flare up. He then explains that Torah clothes a person in anavah, which is like a coat that can be put on and taken off, and that it takes da'as to know when to use it.

title.en: Torah prepares a person to be a tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav explains that Torah lishmah prepares a person to be a tzaddik even in matters beyond his control, such as forbidden food that dulls his feeling for kedushah. Since one cannot be careful enough, tzaddikim need siyata dishmaya, and he tells of a tzaddik who sensed any doubt in his food and would not eat a questionable piece of chicken.

title.en: The pancake that squirted

summary.en: The Rav tells of a gadol who, at a Rav's lunch, became absorbed in pilpul and did not eat a pancake that turned out to have been made with butter in a fleishig pan. He said it was not ruach hakodesh: the hot fat squirted into his face while he learned, so he concluded it could not be kosher.

title.en: A Rebbe and the untoveled dishes

summary.en: The Rav retells a story he heard from an elderly Yerushalmi in his shul in Williamsburg: a Rebbe in Yerushalayim came to eat at a beardless yerei shamayim, did not touch the fish, and discovered that the dishes, borrowed from a chassid with a beard and peyos, had not been toveled. The Rebbe told the host what each would be asked in the next world.

title.en: The gabbai and the knife

summary.en: The Rav tells a story he heard from Mr. Singer, a man in the shul of his youth: a Rebbe's gabbai, a great tzaddik, stayed with Mr. Singer's father for Shabbos, and refused a new knife that the boy had claimed to tovel but had not, because the river was frozen. The Rav concludes that Torah conditions a person to be a tzaddik and gives him all the help he needs.

title.en: Gladdening people: the chassidim's love

summary.en: On the second side the Rav returns to the Mishnah: one who learns Torah lishmah gladdens Hashem and people. He brings a letter printed at the end of the Noam Elimelech in which a man describes to his father-in-law, who feared the chassidim, how they love each other like brothers, so that one cannot tell whose children are whose. He then notes the Gemara's harsh words about learning not lishmah.

title.en: Power misused: the four animals

summary.en: After a long poorly recorded stretch, the Rav compares Torah to a great power that blesses when used well and destroys when misused, and notes that when people are pleased with a person Hashem is pleased with him. He brings the Medrash that the four animals with one kosher sign stand for the four exiles, and explains that a good sign used for evil makes them worse, as with one who learns without good middos.

title.en: Rachamim after the ir hanidachas

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk in this week's parsha that after destroying an ir hanidachas Hashem will give rachamim, and the Ohr HaChaim's account of the king's executioners who said killing gives them pleasure. He applies it: if one is not a mensch, his learning makes him worse, and a talmid chacham must let others live as long as they do no harm.

title.en: The yetzer hara called 'Yesh'

summary.en: The Rav tells a parable: the yetzer hara, the original serpent, complained that nobody listens to him because everyone recognizes him, so he changed his name, finally to 'Yesh', and went around the batei midrash and yeshivos, so that the more people learned the more of a 'yesh' they became. He concludes that Torah is meant to bring anavah and make a person a mensch, and that a real oved Hashem never has bad middos.

title.en: Before Moshiach: throwing off restraint

summary.en: The Rav describes how just before Moshiach people want to throw off every moral restraint and do whatever they want, citing the Gemara that before Moshiach chutzpah will increase and the generation will be like a dog. Against this he praises the refined speech and conduct of a talmid chacham as the Rambam defines it.

title.en: Unusable audio at the end

summary.en: The last minutes of the recording are not transcribed; the ASR produced only a fragment and repeated filler.

catalogTitle: אם אפי' קל שבקלים מוסר נפש לה'' למה היא חוטא? תירוץ - זה שטות.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, on Tanya chapter 19, that even the lowest Jew is ready to give his life rather than deny Hashem because of the hidden love in his soul, and that he sins only because a spirit of folly enters him.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the Tanya's teaching that every Jew carries a hidden love for Hashem, so that even sinners give their lives for kiddush Hashem. This love comes from the chochmah of the G-dly soul, which in a sinner is like a glowing coal covered with ash. He then asks: if such a person is ready to die for Hashem, why does he sin all his life? The answer is folly, as people smoke knowing it shortens their lives. Only the spreading light of chochmah is in exile; its essence sleeps and wakes at a test of faith. He ties this to Adar and Purim, a month of hidden miracles for Jews whose faith is hidden. The Tanya adds that a Jew gives his life even over words or deeds he does not mean, a fear contained within love, like a mother holding her child on the stairs. The Rav ends with a gloss of the Tzemach Tzedek limiting this rule.

en: Every Jew, even the lowest sinner, has a hidden love for Hashem that comes out when he is tested and ready to die rather than convert.
A Jew sins only because a spirit of folly enters him; sin is no more logical than smoking while knowing it kills.
Only the spreading of the soul's chochmah into the body is in exile; its root and essence stay untouched and only sleep.
Adar and Purim are the time of hidden miracles and of revealing the hidden love of even the lowest Jews.
A Jew gives his life even over a denial in speech or action he does not mean, because he fears being cut off from Hashem.
This fear is a fear contained within love, like a mother who grips her child on the stairs because she loves it.

title.en: The hidden love and the spirit of folly

summary.en: The Rav reviews that every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem, so that even the lowest are ready to die rather than convert. He reads the Tanya: this love comes from the chochmah of the G-dly soul, hidden in a sinner like a coal under ash, and covered by the kelipah through a spirit of folly.

title.en: Why he sins: it is folly

summary.en: The Rav asks why one who would die for Hashem sins all his life, and answers that it is folly. He compares it to smoking, which people do although they know it shortens life, something no animal would do, and traces this folly to Adam eating from the Tree of Knowledge.

title.en: Only the spreading light is in exile

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's distinction: only the spreading of chochmah into the body is in exile and darkened, while its root stays out of exile and only sleeps. At a test of faith it wakes, and even a simple Jew stands firm without reasons he can explain.

title.en: Nissan and Adar: open and hidden miracles

summary.en: Bringing the Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of world, time and soul, the Rav contrasts Nissan, the month of open miracles, with Adar, the month of hidden ones. He shows that the Megillah's miracles are all within nature, yet perfectly timed by a higher hand.

title.en: Amalek, emunah and the melting of kelipah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Purim miracles were for sinful Jews whom Amalek could attack, and that Adar is for the lowest generation, whose faith is hidden. Moshe's strength against Amalek was emunah, and at a test of faith all the kelipos melt before Hashem like wax.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh over the garments of denial

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's point that the awakened love will not let the kelipah touch even the garments of thought, speech and action. Even a simple Jew forced to bow or to declare belief in idolatry gives his life, though he could say he does not mean it.

title.en: Fear contained within love

summary.en: The Rav asks how fear fits a teaching about hidden love, and answers with the Tanya's 'fear contained in love': a mother grips her child on the stairs out of fear that comes from her love. So a Jew fears harming his love for Hashem, by nature and by faith.

title.en: The Purim decree and the merit of the Jews

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Haman's decree came because the Jews bowed to the image, and says the merit pleaded for them is their hidden love, which is above reason and is revealed in Adar. This is why one drinks on Purim and why simple Jews rejoice on Purim more than scholars.

title.en: Summary and the Tzemach Tzedek's exception

summary.en: The Rav sums up that even the lowest Jew gives his life rather than deny Hashem, even in speech or action alone, because he feels it would tear him from his root. He then reports a gloss of the Tzemach Tzedek, which he heard of but did not see, that this has exceptions.

catalogTitle: אלו שעברו על חלב עכו"ם' חמץ בפסח' ונדה לא ימסרו נפשם על קידוש ה'. כל עבירה היא ע"ז ממש.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why sins tied to idolatry, like chametz on Pesach and niddah, weaken a Jew's readiness to give his life for Hashem, and begins Tanya chapter 20, which shows that every sin is rooted in idolatry and that Hashem remains exactly as He was before creation.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the previous chapter: even a simple Jew will give his life rather than bow to an idol, because idolatry tears him from his root. He then cites the hagahos of the Tzemach Tzedek, as he heard it: one who eats chametz on Pesach, drinks chalav akum, or is not careful with niddah may lose that readiness, since these sins are bound up with idolatry, and he uses this to explain a puzzling Tosafos about a tzaddik who drank wine a gentile had touched. He contrasts the soldier's trained self-sacrifice with the inner instinct of even the lowest Jews. Turning to Tanya chapter 20, he explains that Anochi and Lo yihyeh contain the whole Torah, that every sin is rooted in idolatry, and that everything is drawn to its source, a sense sins numb. He then explains Hashem's absolute oneness, unchanged by creation, through the parable of speech and thought within the soul.

en: A Jew will give his life rather than even outwardly bow to an idol, because he senses that idolatry tears him from Hashem, his root, and this is above reason.
Sins connected to idolatry, such as chametz on Pesach, chalav akum and niddah, can take away a Jew's readiness for mesiras nefesh.
Every sin is truly rooted in idolatry, so a Jew should be as ready to overcome his nature for any sin as for idolatry; he fails only because he does not understand this.
Anochi and Lo yihyeh lecha include the whole Torah: every positive mitzvah stems from emunah and every prohibition from idolatry, its opposite.
Everything is instinctively drawn to its source, so all creation and above all Jews are drawn to Hashem; sins dull this sense like an anesthetic.
Hashem is One exactly as before creation; creation brings no change in Him, since everything is as nothing before Him.

speech, thought and the essence of the soul

title.en: Self-sacrifice and the three exceptions

summary.en: The Rav recalls that every Jew will give his life rather than bow to an idol, since idolatry is above reason and tears him from his root. He brings, as he heard it, the hagahos of the Tzemach Tzedek: one who eats chametz on Pesach, drinks chalav akum or is lax with niddah may not have this strength, because these sins are tied to idolatry.

title.en: A puzzling Tosafos; Jewish versus trained self-sacrifice

summary.en: The Rav tells a story from Tosafos in Avodah Zarah about a tzaddik who drank wine a gentile had touched to annoy him, and who later gave his life al kiddush Hashem, and says the Tzemach Tzedek's words explain it. He then contrasts soldiers and others who are trained to die for a cause with Jews, even the lowest, whose hidden love would not let them be torn from Hashem.

title.en: Every sin is rooted in idolatry

summary.en: The Rav outlines the coming chapters: being ready to die for idolatry while stumbling in other sins is foolishness, because every sin is rooted in idolatry. If a Jew understood this, he would overcome his nature for every sin as he does for idolatry.

title.en: Anochi and Lo yihyeh include the whole Torah

summary.en: The Rav begins Tanya chapter 20: the first two commandments, heard from Hashem Himself, include the whole Torah, the positive mitzvos stemming from emunah and the prohibitions from idolatry. To explain this, the Tanya first speaks of Hashem's oneness, and the Rav explains 'all believe that He is alone' with the Rosh Hashanah piyut, where Hashem searches the hidden places of the heart.

title.en: Drawn to the source; the ox knows its owner

summary.en: The Rav explains that everything is drawn to its source, as hunger and thirst draw a person to what he lacks, so all creation is drawn to Hashem. Through the ox that knows its owner, the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and the Canaanite slave who may eat terumah, he shows how a person's soul extends into his possessions, and explains that sins numb a Jew's sense of Hashem like an anesthetic.

title.en: Alone as before creation: yachid umeyuchad

summary.en: Reading the Tanya, the Rav explains that Hashem is alone after creation exactly as before, with no change. Physical things occupy a place and exclude another, and every thing can be divided, so nothing created is truly one; Hashem's 'echad' is a oneness without limit, and before Him all the worlds are as nothing.

title.en: The parable of speech, thought and the soul

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's parable: one word is nothing compared to the power of speech, still less to thought, and less still to the essence of the soul. He shows that a person thinks in a language, but the first stirring, like hunger or a desire, comes from the soul itself before any letters, as with an animal that wants food without planning.

catalogTitle: הקב"ה ודיבורו אחד ממש. אלא לגבי נבראים יש צמצומים.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 21, the Rav explains that Hashem's speech is not separate from Him as human speech is; it is one with His essence, and the tzimtzumim and concealments exist only from the side of the creations who receive.

abstract.en: The Rav places chapter 21 within a five-chapter unit showing that any sin, even the smallest, cuts a Jew off from Hashem like idolatry, since Anochi and Lo yihyeh are the roots of all the mitzvos; the Ba'al Shem Tov, he notes, said this in one word. He then explains that human speech is communication that separates from the speaker and is felt, which the Ba'al haTanya could sense and which a tape recorder now shows, and he tells the story of the Ba'al haTanya and the king in prison. Hashem's speech, by contrast, is not separate from Him; it is called speech only as a mashal, as Dovid compared himself to a desert bird only in his loneliness. Like a person's desire in the heart before it becomes thought, Hashem's speech is one with His essence, and nothing changed through creation. Only from the side of the recipients are there tzimtzumim and hester panim; for Him darkness is like light, and like the kamtza whose shell is part of itself, His garments are Himself.

en: Chapters 20-24 of Tanya show that every sin, even the smallest, cuts a person off from Hashem like idolatry, because Anochi and Lo yihyeh are the roots of all the mitzvos.
Human speech is communication that leaves the speaker and becomes something separate from him; Hashem's speech is not separate from Him at all.
Hashem's word is called 'speech' only as a mashal: as human speech reveals hidden thought to a listener, His speech is the revelation of His light to the creations.
Like a person's desire in the heart before it becomes letters of thought, Hashem's speech is one with His essence, and creation changed nothing for Him.
The tzimtzumim and hester panim exist only from the side of the recipients, so that they can bear the light; for Hashem darkness is like light and His garments are Himself.

title.en: Every sin as idolatry: the Ba'al Shem Tov's word

summary.en: The Rav places the chapter within a five-chapter unit explaining that any sin cuts one off from Hashem like idolatry, since Anochi and Lo yihyeh are the roots of all positive and negative mitzvos. He says these are deep chapters he will go through quickly, and notes that the Ba'al Shem Tov said all this in one word on 'and you will turn away and serve other gods'.

title.en: Human speech and Hashem's speech

summary.en: The Rav explains that human speech is the communication that carries one person's thought over to another, as 'yadber amim' means leading over, and it separates from the speaker. Hashem's speech is not separate from Him; it is called speech only as a mashal. He contrasts the Rishonim's answer that a Sanhedrin is fixed but its ruling goes out as separate, which cannot apply to Hashem.

title.en: Speech is felt: the Ba'al haTanya in prison

summary.en: Reading the opening of chapter 21, the Rav explains that the Ba'al haTanya, with his fine senses, could feel the speech that leaves a person, which a tape recorder shows today. He tells how the king came in disguise to the Ba'al haTanya in prison and tested him on the time and on the number of coins from the table to the ceiling.

title.en: Why it is called speech: a mashal

summary.en: The Rav explains that nothing is separate from Hashem, since His glory fills the earth, and His speech is not like ours just as His thoughts are not ours. He asks why it is called speech at all and answers that it is a mashal for revelation, like Dovid's comparison to a desert bird, and that the ten utterances and all of Tanach are His speech. He then shows that human speech expresses thought, and thought itself comes from a deeper root.

title.en: Desire before thought: speech one with His essence

summary.en: The Rav explains that every thought is stirred by a desire in the heart, as when a person wants to eat, before it becomes letters of thought. For a person, speech is a power of a power; for Hashem, speech is His very essence, united with Him as the desire is united with a person's self, and there is no change in Him through creation.

title.en: Two points of view: Creator and recipients

summary.en: The Rav says the Nefesh HaChaim discusses this at length: no place is empty of Hashem, yet a person relates to his things as real. There are two perspectives: from the Creator's side only His glory fills the earth, while from the recipients' side we live in a world of imagination. He asks how anything can exist after creation if before it there was only Hashem, and answers that for Him it is all the same.

title.en: Tzimtzumim only for the receivers; the kamtza

summary.en: Rereading the text, the Rav explains that the many tzimtzumim and the hester panim exist so the creations can receive the light without being nullified, but before Hashem darkness is like light. With the mashal of the kamtza whose shell is part of itself, and the halachah that one's own hand is not a head covering while another's hand is, he shows that Hashem's garments are His own essence. He closes by saying he will stop here and review.

catalogTitle: דרשה בבית האסורים: English: Freedom in Prison. אידיש: גודל תענוג השכינה מעבודה בעמקי הקליפות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the light Hashem created on the twenty-fifth of Elul is true freedom, the freedom from the yetzer hara to serve Hashem, and that even from the lowest places a Jew can crown Hashem as King.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the twenty-fifth of Elul, the day the world was created, and the words 'Yehi or', 'let there be light', which he says are repeated each year on this day. Light, he explains, means happiness and contentment, and above all liberty. Dovid HaMelech calls prisoners those who sit in darkness, but the greatest imprisonment is to be bound by the yetzer hara; the whole world, in his words, is a big prison, because people who think they are free must obey their bad passions. When Hashem said 'let there be light' He meant freedom to serve Him, which every person inwardly desires. The Rav speaks of the awaited Rosh Hashanah when all mankind will be free to serve Hashem, and blesses his listeners. He then turns to Yiddish; through heavy garbling one can hear that service from the lowest places brings great joy above, and that a Jew should proclaim 'HaMelech' wherever he is.

en: Each year on the twenty-fifth of Elul, the day of creation, the creation and the 'Yehi or' are repeated.
Light means happiness and contentment, and its most precious form is liberty.
The greatest imprisonment is being a prisoner of the yetzer hara, and in this sense the whole world is a big prison.
'Let there be light' meant freedom to serve Hashem and follow the good inclinations every person carries inside.
The world awaits a Rosh Hashanah when all mankind will be free, subservient to no will but Hashem's.

title.en: The light of creation is liberty

summary.en: The Rav opens with the twenty-fifth of Elul, when the world was created and Hashem said 'Yehi or', and explains that light means happiness and above all liberty. He says the greatest prison is the yetzer hara, and that the whole world is a big prison of people who think they are free.

title.en: Freedom to serve Hashem and the awaited Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'let there be light' meant freedom to serve Hashem, which every human being inwardly desires, and speaks of the coming Rosh Hashanah when all mankind will be free of the yetzer hara. He blesses the listeners and announces that he will continue in Yiddish.

title.en: Serving Hashem from the depths

summary.en: In a Yiddish discourse that the ASR largely garbled, the Rav speaks of the joy above when a Jew serves Hashem from the lowest places, among idol worshippers and outside Eretz Yisrael. On Rosh Hashanah, he says, a Jew should proclaim 'HaMelech' wherever he is, since even a prison is a place to serve Hashem.
